pr_title: Update EIP-8142: Bib columns propagation
author: frisitano
body: I wonder if there's a way to signal to peers that a node in a custody group exclusively wants the execution payload and is not interested in the remaining rows. This could possibly be done via a `CustodyIndex` configuration. My thinking here is that the peers of the custody column topic should not send `IHAVE` messages to peers in that topic who are only interested in the execution payload row - this could save some additional bandwidth, but I am uncertain about the magnitude of the savings and the complexity of the libpw2p design.

pr_title: Update EIP-8142: Bib columns propagation
author: kamilsa
body:
> I wonder if there's a way to signal to peers that a node in a custody group exclusively wants the execution payload and is not interested in the remaining rows.

This is exactly what partial messages allows us to do. Peers exchange bitmaps of what rows they are interested in.

> My thinking here is that the peers of the custody column topic should not send IHAVE messages to peers in that topic who are only interested in the execution payload row - this could save some additional bandwidth

It is possible to send custody columns only to peers who are interested in full columns during critical path (so peers are able to attest faster), and then start also advertising availability bitmaps to non-custody peers.

Keep in mind, that once mandatory proofs are landed we don't need to keep subscription to all columns, so this is only for transition period to speed up execution payload propagation

pr_title: Update EIP-8142: Bib columns propagation
author: frisitano
body:
I think even after mandatory proofs, we will want a mechanism to fetch the payload over the network for peers that perform re-execution, without relying on the EL p2p network.

I think we can iron out some of these details later if needed but I think your baseline proposal makes sense in any case.

pr_title: Update EIP-8141: Add explicit second dimension for state gas to frames
author: jochem-brouwer
body:
What happens if we introduce another gas dimension? How would we pack this in frame txs?

Is it necessary to split gas limit in these two dimensions? I would initially say that this is not necessary: all gas is execution gas. If a state operation happens and it gets cancelled, then this moves into the reservoir. However, not allowing this splitting means that a tx which has an intended split of execution/state gas does not fit in the block anymore because one (or both) of the gas dimensions would exceed the block gas limit. So I guess there is indeed reason to add this feature here.

Only worried if we go to multidimensional gas, then this is not forward compatible, and then we need to introduced "typed frame transactions" 😜

pr_title: Update EIP-8141: Add explicit second dimension for state gas to frames
author: jochem-brouwer
body:
```suggestion
Each frame incurs a fixed CALL execution-context overhead (100) plus `G_log` (375) for the receipt sub-entry it produces, giving `FRAME_TX_PER_FRAME_COST = 475`. The execution-context component covers context setup, mode dispatch, and the two-dimensional gas accounting at the frame boundary, analogous to the fixed overhead of a CALL. The `G_log` component covers the `[status, execution_gas_used, state_gas_used, logs]` receipt sub-entry that each frame adds to the transaction receipt, which must be serialized, hashed into the receipt trie, and proven by ZK-EVM implementations. Cold/warm access costs for the frame's target account are charged within the frame's own `execution_gas_limit` through the normal EVM warm/cold accounting, not through the per-frame cost.
```

pr_title: Update EIP-8141: Add explicit second dimension for state gas to frames
author: jochem-brouwer
body:
```suggestion
Notes: Nonce assumes < 65536 prior sends. Fees assume < 1099 gwei. Validation frame target is 1 byte because target is `tx.sender`. Validation gas assumes <= 65,536 gas. Validation frame value is zero. Execution frame target is encoded directly as the destination address. Execution frame value assumes a compact 5-byte encoding. The execution frame data is empty for a plain ETH transfer. The signature is a secp256k1 entry with empty `msg` using a 65-byte ECDSA signature. Blob fields assume no blobs (empty list, zero max fee). State gas limits are zero, assuming the destination exists; a transfer that creates a new account instead requires a ``STATE_BYTES_PER_NEW_ACCOUNT × CPSB = 183,600` state gas budget on the execution frame (three additional bytes).
```

(the 183,600 should be defined as a constant somewhere, now it is a magic number for readers not deep in EIP-8037)

pr_title: Update EIP-8141: Add explicit second dimension for state gas to frames
author: jochem-brouwer
body:
Saw this PR and gave it a read, some comments.

Allowing state gas introspection to other (earlier) frames means we can (in some specific cases) verify if such frame created a slot. This thus adds a subset of journal introspection to the EVM. 
We could fix this by pinning the state gas used of previous frames to the value at the start of the currently executing frame. Any refills can thus not be measured by the EVM, while they are accounted for in the end.

The other thing is that not allowing state gas to be paid with execution gas also means that deep call frames can exhaust all state gas and therefore not allow later operations to create state (as this would attempt to put state gas below 0). This is something to think about, it might be the same argument for sending all your gas to untrusted accounts, but this definitely is something which "rogue contracts" can use to attack. The only way to then regain the "rights" to create state is to revert the current frame and therefore rollback the state creation by the rogue account.
Note that in EIP-8037 execution gas would pay for it if the state gas / state reservoir is empty.
Also note that we now have two gas journaling modes, one for frame txs and the other for non-frame txs.

Lemme know if you have some questions if I made a comment which is unclear 😄 👍 

Exciting work!! 😄 🚀

pr_title: Update EIP-8297: Delete leaves on zeroization
author: kevaundray
body:
ah yeah I was saying something slightly different; the "zero means delete" rule _could_ either live in the trie or in the stf.

I initially thought adding deletions meant we would allow the following behaviour on the trie:

```
insert(key, value)
delete(key)
```

and then to actually do a deletion, we have something like this in the stf:

```
if storage value == 0:
    trie.delete(key)
else:
    trie.insert(key, encode(value))
```

pr_title: Update EIP-8297: Delete leaves on zeroization
author: kevaundray
body:
The pros of the above method is that the trie is left generic and doesn't encode anything special.

The alternative which is what I understand from this change is the following:

```
insert(key, value != 0)
insert(key, 0) // This is a deletion or a noop if the key is not already present
```

The pros of the above is that the invariant "zero means delete" is encoded in the trie itself

pr_title: Update EIP-8297: Delete leaves on zeroization
author: CPerezz
body:
All-zero code chunks contradict the new rule. `chunkify_code` zero-pads code to a multiple of 31 and sets byte 0 to the PUSHDATA count, which is 0 outside PUSHDATA. So:
```
 code = 0x00                      (one byte: STOP)
 code_size   = 1
 chunk count = ceil(1/31) = 1
 chunk 0     = 0x00 ‖ 0x00×31  =  32 zero bytes
```

Here we say 32-zero-byte value MUST NOT be present; the Code section says chunk count is `ceil(code_size/31)` and says nothing about skipping. 

We should exempt code-chunk keys. As we can have a chunk of a contract that is actually all zero for example. And this isn't an issue for state-size as we don't care at all about duplication (we de-duplicate).

pr_title: Update EIP-8297: Delete leaves on zeroization
author: misilva73
body:
Good catch! I went the other way on the fix though. I kept the rule uniform and just said so in "Code", rather than exempting code keys. Two reasons:

1. The exemption isn't actually a zone. `CODE_OFFSET = 128`, so chunks 0–127 sit in `ACCOUNT_ZONE` alongside `BASIC_DATA`, `code_hash` and storage slots 0–63 — so it's a sub-index range, and fixtures, BAL replay and state-dump rebuilds all have to know about it.

2. And nothing breaks: `code_size` delimits the code, not chunk presence. Reconstruction derives each chunk's key from `i`, so an absent chunk reads back as the zeros it would have held — same as a zero storage slot. Checked the round-trip on a 3-chunk code with an all-zero middle chunk, byte-exact.

pr_title: Update EIP-8333: use the attestation deadline, not a specific fraction of a slot
author: lodekeeper
body:
Approving as an EIP-8333 author.

The change is correct and an improvement. Swapping the hardcoded "one third of a slot" for "the attestation deadline" keeps the wording accurate across forks: today the deadline sits at 1/3 of a slot (`ATTESTATION_DUE_BPS = 3333`), but post-Gloas it moves to 1/4 (`ATTESTATION_DUE_BPS_GLOAS = 2500`), so the fixed fraction would go stale after ePBS. The "gains a full slot of additional propagation time" phrasing is also precise — anchoring to the boundary block moves the target exactly one slot earlier, independent of where the deadline falls within the slot.

Thanks @jihoonsong!

author: eth-bot
body: ✅ All reviewers have approved.

pr_title: Update EIP-7906: Add POST_TX enforcement to security considerations
author: forshtat
body:
```suggestion
While `POST_TX` frames dictate how assertions are executed, there is no explicit protocol-level requirement that a transaction *must* include a `POST_TX` frame. Smart accounts aiming to use `POST_TX` frames must explicitly configure their `VERIFY` frame's validation logic to strictly require the presence of their specific `POST_TX` frame in every transaction they approve without any mechanist that could allow circumventing this requirement.
```

pr_title: Update EIP-7906: Add POST_TX enforcement to security considerations
author: forshtat
body:
```suggestion
Because a transaction can contain multiple `POST_TX` frames, and they are guaranteed to form a contiguous suffix at the end of the transaction, the smart account can iterate backwards to locate its required assertion frame. 
```

pr_title: Update EIP-7906: Add POST_TX enforcement to security considerations
author: forshtat
body:
```suggestion
It is critical that the expected target of all `POST_TX` frames is an immutable, non-upgradeable contract. If the assertion contract were upgradeable, a malicious transaction could potentially upgrade it during execution to bypass the security checks. Only as long as the `VERIFY` frame executes *before* any state changes are made, checking the POST_TX` frame target during validation guarantees the transaction will be evaluated against the intended immutable policy.
```

pr_title: Update EIP-8141: recognize the canonical paymaster by stable identity, not exact bytecode match
author: AnkushinDaniil
body:
Thanks @svlachakis @benaadams, agreed - closing this.

Pinned-hash recognition is carried in full by #12012 now, with a real referent, and the bytecode-drift point is covered by SETCODEFROM (EIP-8298) cloning + the per-fork code hash. The 7702 half doesn't hold up: a delegated account keeps a live key that can move the balance with a normal tx outside the tracked set, and any EOA could self-delegate to look canonical. #12012 is the right home.

Note: this is the original text from line 43, except with some changes. 

This is the reverse diff, so all additions are the removals what I have done:


```suggestion
A chain may satisfy this requirement by either of the following means that results in the account above: deploying the factory with an ordinary transaction (for example, its keyless creation transaction) where the chain's gas parameters permit it, or including the account in the genesis state with a nonce equal to `1`. ```
```

pr_title: Update EIP-8141: canonical P256 sender account for no-simulation admission
author: svlachakis
body:
Concept looks right and follows the canonical paymaster precedent cleanly, and it closes a real gap since default code is SECP256K1-only. Two things worth pinning before this leaves draft:

- Where the configured credential lives. I think it has to be in the account's storage, and since admission reads it, that slot is part of the mempool dependency set (rotating the credential invalidates pending transactions) and the storage layout needs to be normative per canonical version, same as the canonical paymaster's signer.
- If this and #12001 both land, #12001's enumeration of code-match species needs a one-line amendment to include this account. No textual conflict, whoever merges second can do the touch-up.

pr_title: Update EIP-8141: canonical P256 sender account for no-simulation admission
author: AnkushinDaniil
body: Agreed on both. Pinned the credential location in the spec text: it is held in the account's storage, the slot is part of the mempool dependency set (so a rotation invalidates the sender's pending txs), and its layout is normative per canonical version - same as the canonical paymaster's signer. And yes, whoever lands second amends #12001's code-match species list to include this account; no textual conflict.

pr_title: Update EIP-8141: canonical P256 sender account for no-simulation admission
author: lightclient
body:
We actually had P256 as a possible signature type in the default code, but we removed it because we realized it actually creates a weird class of account. It isn't a smart account so it can't make a 1271-sig, can't use `permit`, can't handle callbacks for erc-721, etc. It also can't deploy code for itself! Yes, we could potentially address some of these issues, but at the end of the day P256 is not a top-level account the protocol supports. Just a cryptographic operation we provide optimized support for.

So I am generally against this.

pr_title: Update EIP-8141: canonical P256 sender account for no-simulation admission
author: AnkushinDaniil
body: Updated per the broader family-robustness discussion: the canonical P256 account is now recognized by **stable identity** - an EIP-7702 delegation to a reserved `CANONICAL_P256_ACCOUNT` address (versioned by address), or a code hash pinned for the active fork - rather than by exact runtime-bytecode equality against an unpinned implementation. This keeps it versionable and avoids propagation fragmentation from toolchain bytecode drift, and it addresses the concern that canonicalizing an opaque wallet blob is the wrong axis: what is canonical is the P256 scheme verification at a reserved address, with the account being the credential shell (credential still in own storage, per the earlier note). Pairs with a parallel proposal to recognize the canonical paymaster the same way.

pr_title: Update EIP-8141: canonical P256 sender account for no-simulation admission
author: AnkushinDaniil
body:
You are right, and this lines up with where our own analysis landed: P256 is a cryptographic operation the protocol optimizes (it is already scheme 0x2), not a top-level account. A P256 "account" that is not a real smart contract is exactly the weird class you describe - no 1271, no permit, no ERC-721 callbacks, no self-deploy.

The clean way to give passkey/P256 users cheap no-simulation admission is a real smart wallet that verifies the P256 scheme and is admitted by a canonical account identity, not a P256 pseudo-account. So I will close this. The identity-not-bytecode recognition it introduced still applies to the canonical paymaster (a real contract) in #12010. Thanks for the catch.

pr_title: Update EIP-8141: specify the APPROVE opcode gas cost
author: svlachakis
body: Agree with the approach. APPROVE is RETURN plus once-per-transaction context effects, and those effects (nonce increment, payer set, fee collection) are exactly what intrinsic cost covers in a standard transaction, so charging nothing extra here is consistent pricing rather than free state writes. Maybe worth one sentence of rationale saying that, to preempt the obvious "why free?" question. Side benefit: this pins the APPROVE term needed for the MAX_VERIFY_GAS arithmetic in #12001's direct evaluation.

pr_title: Update EIP-8141: specify the APPROVE opcode gas cost
author: AnkushinDaniil
body: Good call - added the rationale: the once-per-transaction effects (nonce increment, setting payer, collecting the max cost) are already covered by the frame tx intrinsic cost, same as a standard transaction, so charging nothing extra is consistent pricing rather than a free state write. And agreed, it pins the APPROVE term for the MAX_VERIFY_GAS arithmetic in #12001.

author: AnkushinDaniil
body: Looks correct and it is the right framing - direct evaluation equals simulation exactly when every prefix frame is protocol-defined, and enumerating the minimal dependency set (sender code-hash/nonce, payer code-hash/balance or the paymaster tracked state, EXPIRY_VERIFIER code + deadline, timestamp) is what lets nodes revalidate on new heads without re-execution. pr_title: Add EIP: Offline State Migration to the PBT
author: misilva73
body:
Thanks for the review @CPerezz. All comments addressed across three commits.

**Deletion semantics** (`d33dd4b9`, new **Replay deletion semantics** subsection under BAL-replay):

- **7702 delegation clear.** A code change now recomputes the new code's chunk leaves and deletes stale ones the new code doesn't cover. The delegation case is named: code returns to empty and the 23-byte indicator at sub-index `CODE_OFFSET` (= 128) must be deleted. `code_hash` and basic-data are updated rather than deleted, since a codeless account still commits to the Keccak hash of empty bytecode and `code_size = 0`.
- **Delete-and-merge.** Specified as a **Canonicalization** rule, the exact inverse of the insertion split. A sibling leaf replaces the branch outright; a sibling branch with prefix `q` replaces it with `p || b || q`. Deleting the last leaf gives the empty tree, hash `[0x00] * 32`.
- **Flip at the fork.** Stated explicitly. Deletion is migration-only, from `ANCHOR_BLOCK` until activation. From activation 8297 governs: writing zero stores a zero-valued leaf, distinct from an absent key.

Your second comment turned up a gap I'd missed. `9f44a0f2` scopes deletion to header chunks, since overflow chunks are content-addressed by `code_hash` and shared between contracts with identical bytecode.

**On the swap being unspecified**, you were right, and it was the biggest hole in the document. `2c97c8ad` adds an **Activation** section: no payload-structure change (`stateRoot` keeps its name, position, and type, only the tree changes); the boundary is a single block, not a range; the CL treats `state_root` as opaque bytes, so its only change is fork scheduling; and shadow-root publication ends at activation, with the sidecar removable in a later release.

One difference from your suggestion: instead of mandating an engine-API version bump, it says no new payload field is introduced, so no engine-API change is required here, and any bump is the meta EIP's call. The `newPayloadV2/V3/V4` bumps each tracked a real payload change (withdrawals, blobs, requests), and there isn't one here. Happy to mandate a bump if you disagree.

Separately: EIP-8297 §Fork still points at the EIP-7612 overlay transition, i.e. the online model this EIP replaces. Probably needs fixing on that side.

Also, `SWAP_FORK` is now `PBT_ACTIVATION_FORK`, per jochem's circular-dependency point.

pr_title: Add EIP: Offline State Migration to the PBT
author: kevaundray
body:
```suggestion
An optional design chunked the PBT snapshot at fixed, stem-aligned byte boundaries and ships a manifest of per-chunk hashes inside the byte-canonical artifact. That is deliberately not specified here. The [dual-check](#verification-dual-check) is the sole root of trust: it authenticates the reassembled artifact against `ANCHOR_BLOCK`'s `stateRoot`, so a manifest adds no security. Its only value is download efficiency (partial-download integrity, parallelism, resumption), and the transports already in use for distribution (snap-sync-style peer-to-peer, era-style files, CDNs, torrents) provide exactly that. Specifying a normative chunking scheme would duplicate transport-layer functionality and would force producers to cut boundaries bit-identically merely to keep the in-artifact manifest canonical. Dropping it leaves the artifact as a byte-canonical, PBT-key-sorted leaf stream with a small header, and leaves splitting for transport to the distribution layer, which MAY publish a non-normative chunk-hash index as a download accelerator.
```

pr_title: Add EIP: Offline State Migration to the PBT
author: jochem-brouwer
body:
```suggestion
The full state at a finalized **anchor block `ANCHOR_BLOCK`** is converted off the consensus-critical path. The result is distributed as a byte-canonical, verifiable **PBT snapshot**. That PBT snapshot is caught up to the chain tip by replaying Block-Level Access Lists (BALs) ([EIP-7928](./eip-7928.md)), and it is made canonical at a single EL+CL hard fork **`SWAP_FORK`**. Both trees are maintained through a transition window until finality after `SWAP_FORK`.
```

pr_title: Add EIP: Offline State Migration to the PBT
author: jochem-brouwer
body:
```suggestion
The PBT snapshot is large (~100+ GB) and distributed off-chain. In principle this could be a vector for serving corrupted state. The dual-check verification neutralizes it. Internal PBT consistency plus consensus anchoring against `ANCHOR_BLOCK`'s `stateRoot` lets any node reject a bad artifact without trusting the source, including a fresh node. The root of trust is `ANCHOR_BLOCK`'s `stateRoot`, taken from the node's own header chain, so a fabricated but internally self-consistent package (fake leaves matching a fake `pbtRoot`) still fails consensus anchoring. Integrity checking on partial downloads is handled by the distribution transport (e.g. torrent piece hashes, Transport Layer Security (TLS), CDN checksums), letting a node drop a bad segment on arrival rather than after full reassembly; a malicious distributor serving altered bytes that pass those transport checks is still caught by the dual-check once the artifact is reassembled.
```

Note that we can directly verify the inner node correctness by hashing those to the top of the trie.
This means that we can verify once we got a specific node set if those nodes are correct. If it is not (malicious peer), then ban the peer.
Note that the malicious peer will publish all leafs for a verification except the final one, so we are unable to determine the validity of the previously sent items.

We dont have to spec this of course, we can also use existing solutions.

pr_title: Add EIP: Offline State Migration to the PBT
author: jochem-brouwer
body:
Account deletion is not possible (SELFDESTRUCT only in same tx).
If an account exists, then it has either a balance, nonce (or code) per https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-161. Empty accounts (no balance, nonce, code, storage) do not exist in MPT per https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-7523

If the account exists with balance, then if we clear balance this is either done by tx (this bumps the nonce to nonzero), or via the EIP-7702 delegation. But, the delegation sets code and also bumps the nonce. The nonce is strictly increasing.
Therefore "account deletion" is not possible (in current fork, and also since EIP-7523 + EIP-6780 "SELFDESTRUCT only in same transaction" https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-6780 )

This uses an RFC 2119 keyword outside of Specifications which might indicate new specs here. Please check or lowercase it.


```suggestion
Shadow-root publication stays a should and out of consensus. Enforcing it as a block-validity rule would require every validator to compute the PBT post-state root for every block, putting PBT construction back on the consensus-critical path — the exact property the offline model exists to avoid, and re-introducing the two-trees-consensus-live attack surface. The intended mechanism is therefore an out-of-consensus proposer-signed sidecar on a dedicated gossip topic; a missing shadow root dents the coverage metric rather than counting as a divergence, and cross-client agreement accumulates by observation rather than enforcement. The one narrow case where hard enforcement may still be warranted, the final blocks before `SWAP_FORK`, is discussed under [Unvalidated-flip input](#security-considerations).
```

author: jochem-brouwer

```suggestion
- **Execution semantics.** `SWAP_FORK` changes the state commitment **only**. PBT state access nonetheless performs differently from the MPT (e.g. chunk-granular code access, stem warm/cold behavior), so state-access gas costs are repriced in a **separate gas-repricing EIP**. That repricing is out of scope here and must not be bundled into the commitment-only `SWAP_FORK`; witness/statelessness pricing is likewise out of scope, as this migration does not introduce statelessness. The repricing fork's timing depends on benchmarks of PBT versus MPT access performance:
```

pr_title: Add EIP: Offline State Migration to the PBT
author: misilva73
body:
Both halves are now in the text via `8a572819`.

**What the preimages are for.** Not fresh sync. They're the consensus-anchoring half of the dual-check, which every node runs. The PBT is hash-keyed too: 8297 derives a stem from `key_hash(address)` and a storage position from `key_hash(address || tree_index)`, so a PBT leaf carries no preimage of its own and holding the PBT doesn't give you the keys behind it. Anchoring works by re-hashing the leaves under the MPT schema and checking the result against `ANCHOR_BLOCK`'s header `stateRoot`, and that's impossible without the preimages. So snap-syncing the PBT isn't sufficient: it gives you leaves, but no way to tie them to a consensus-committed root, since no PBT root appears in any header before activation. There's also a second consumer, self-converters on hash-keyed clients. The Preimages section now says all of this up front.

**On the duplication.** You're right that slot keys repeat, but the repetition is concentrated in low-numbered slots. Most storage keys are mapping-derived and unique to one account, so global dedup saves less than it looks like it should. Two changes in that commit:

- Slot keys are now canonical RLP integers with leading zero bytes stripped, so slot 0 is the empty string and slot 1 is a single byte. That reclaims most of what the low-numbered slots were wasting, which is exactly where the duplication lives.
- The grouping choice is now stated as deliberate rather than left implicit. Your alternative needs the client to build `hash(slot) -> slot` as a global lookup table, and at mainnet scale that has to be resident while converting. Grouping under the account instead lets a converter stream one account's storage trie at a time. Trading some on-disk redundancy for bounded converter memory seemed the better side of that.

> Put plainly, the online path asks every state consumer to support three state models: MPT, then hybrid, then PBT. The offline path asks for two: MPT, then PBT. The middle one is the expensive one. It is the only one that is not a plain tree lookup, and the only one built for a bounded window and then maintained anyway.

Light clients are now in the consumer list in both the Motivation and the Rationale, alongside indexers, RPC providers, cross-chain bridges, and dApps. The proof-sensitivity point is covered in two places: **Simpler state proofs** in the Rationale (offline keeps a single canonical root at all times, so no consumer ever straddles two commitments) and **On-chain proof consumers** in Backwards Compatibility, which flags this as the longest-lead-time dependency of the migration.

Fair, and it's a deliberate deferral rather than an oversight. The line is drawn at what the migration's safety argument depends on.

Specified here: attesters are the source, roots are signed with the validator key, publication is out of consensus and a `SHOULD`, and a missing root dents a coverage metric rather than counting as a divergence. Deferred: wire format, aggregation, timing, EL-to-CL plumbing.

```suggestion
**No on-chain observability of the conversion.** This is the second cost. An overlay computes the new root in consensus, so its correctness is observed on-chain as it proceeds. Offline conversion happens off-chain, so consensus does not see it before the swap. This EIP recovers that visibility off consensus, through the [shadow-commitment period](#shadow-commitment). Attesters publish signed per-block PBT roots while consensus still runs on the MPT, so divergence is visible and attributable before the swap depends on it. The substitute is still weaker than in-consensus observation, because publication is not enforced. What gets observed is coverage over voluntary reports, not a validity condition every node must satisfy. One residual exposure remains: a converter bug confined to the final pre-fork blocks, whose activated PBT root consensus never validates. It is addressed under [Unvalidated-flip input](#unvalidated-flip-input).
```

```suggestion
Replay does need one thing execution does not: the ability to delete a leaf, specified under [replay deletion semantics](#replay-deletion-semantics). author: CPerezz
```

- For a Core EIP whose entire purpose is the swap, the swap itself is unspecified. Maybe we should add something more detailed/precise ("no payload-structure change, an engine-API version bump per normal fork convention, the consensus layer treating the root opaquely"). And unsure, but should we hint the removal of the "monitoring/telemetry" in CL via either attestations or whatever other mechanism we decide for. So that at least we briefly mention it.
-  A converter reading MPT accounts emits two leaves for every account (BASIC_DATA at sub-index 0, CODE_HASH at sub-index 1, holding keccak256(b"") for EOAs). 
A replayer creating a fresh EOA from a BAL that carries only a balance change emits one. Since keccak256(b"") is non-zero, the zero-as-absence rule keeps it present, so the two trees are not bit-identical — and this fires on the very first plain transfer to a new address after the anchor. This seems a big issue.
Though the fix is simple. On first materialisation of an account, the CODE_HASH leaf MUST be written — keccak256(b"") unless a code_changes entry for that account in the same block says otherwise.

pr_title: Update EIP-8141: clarify decoding, signing, and activation
author: AnkushinDaniil
body:
The strict RLP/field rules are welcome - implementing against them surfaced two gaps in our decoder (we weren't pinning the outer list to exactly nine elements, and weren't checking the `blob_versioned_hashes` KZG version byte), so these tighten real behavior. `compute_sig_hash` not mutating the decoded transaction is the right call - our prototype already streams the elided form into the hasher without touching the decoded object. P256 via EIP-7951 while keeping the 8141 cost also matches.

One consistency point on activation: `EXPIRY_VERIFIER` initializes on "the first block where this EIP is active", but 8250 (#11960, merged) and 8272 initialize on "every block whose parent has `parent.timestamp < FORK_TIMESTAMP`". Could we use the same formulation here, so the three system-contract activations read identically and the reorg-boundary case is unambiguous?

Heads-up: once this lands, 8272's `compute_sig_hash` (already merged in #11959 with the older mutating form) should follow the same non-mutating shape.

pr_title: Update EIP-8141: clarify decoding, signing, and activation
author: soispoke
body: Updated the activation text to apply whenever the EIP applies to a block but not its parent. #11970 already makes EIP-8272 use EIP-8141’s signature hash procedure, so it will inherit the rule that hashing does not modify the decoded transaction. Thanks!

pr_title: Update EIP-8141: clarify decoding, signing, and activation
author: AnkushinDaniil
body: Looks good, thanks - the new wording ("every block where this EIP applies but does not apply to its parent") matches the 8250/8272 formulation, and it's a nicer generalization since it doesn't hard-code the timestamp comparison. And having 8272 inherit 8141's hash procedure via #11970 is cleaner than duplicating it.

pr_title: Update EIP-8141: clarify decoding, signing, and activation
author: svlachakis
body:
@soispoke Strong support for all four pieces, the strict RLP shape and the pure `compute_sig_hash` are exactly what implementations have had to invent independently, and pinning P256 to EIP-7951's validation with the transaction-level cost formalizes current practice. Note it composes with [#11984](https://github.com/ethereum/EIPs/pull/11984) (low-s canonicality on top of the 7951 rules), worth keeping both in view so a merge doesn't drop either.

I think the `EXPIRY_VERIFIER` activation is the part I'm happiest to see: predeploys that genesis tooling has to remember to ship are a real devnet failure mode, we've already tripped over that class of problem with other predeploys, and the in-protocol install removes it. One question for the Rationale: this diverges from the presigned-deployment convention of 7002/7251-style predeploys ("no code at activation → blocks invalid"), so maybe a sentence saying the divergence is intentional and why would keep the two philosophies from reading as accidental.

pr_title: Update EIP-8141: apply charged_gas to fee settlement
author: AnkushinDaniil
body: Reviewed the settlement math and it holds: with `effective_gas_price <= max_fee_per_gas` and `blob_base_fee <= max_fee_per_blob_gas`, `charged_fee <= collected_max_cost` so `payer_escrow_refund >= 0`, and the net block-gas reduction is exactly `charged_gas`. Separating block-gas accounting (`charged_gas`) from the payer escrow (`collected_max_cost`) reads cleanly, and it applies the EIP-7623 floor correctly. LGTM. On the implementation side this is a real change for us - our prototype still uses the old `tx_fee` model (effective price, no blob escrow), so we'll move to this.

With 7623, you may pay a completely unrelated cost. So we needed to compute this max gas value to know what the overall tx limit really should be to make sure it covers worst case data and execution costs.

I removed a few points around the handling of block gas and 1559 since these are not changing with respect to the EIP and it's okay to leave out.

I agree with the expiry margin admission rule and changing expired reference eviction from MAY to SHOULD.

Could we replace that cap with guidance requiring efficient indexing by declared reference and expiry slot, so expiry and reorg eviction remain bounded without restricting application concurrency?

pr_title: Update EIP-8250: exclude KEYED_NONCE_FIRST_USE_GAS from MAX_VERIFY_GAS accounting
author: AnkushinDaniil
body:
Withdrawing this. On reflection, excluding the surcharge from MAX_VERIFY_GAS weakens the protection it provides: the keyed-nonce reads during validation are exempt from EIP-2929/2200 pricing, so KEYED_NONCE_FIRST_USE_GAS is currently the only thing bounding keyed-read amplification in the public mempool. Removing it from the budget lets a transaction force up to MAX_NONCE_KEYS cheap keyed SLOADs during validation.

A better direction is either (a) accept that the public mempool admits ~5 first-use keys (fewer than MAX_NONCE_KEYS) as intended DoS protection and document that, or (b) charge the per-key validation read directly so it counts toward MAX_VERIFY_GAS (16 reads is cheap and stays bounded) while pricing the 20000 state-growth surcharge at execution rather than in the validation budget. I'll rework along (b) if that seems right. Thanks.

pr_title: Update EIP-8141: note sponsor repayment reversibility and batch the repayment in Example 3
author: svlachakis
body:
```suggestion
- Frame 1: Inspects signature metadata in `tx.signatures` if needed, and checks that the next frame is an ERC-20 send of the right size to the sponsor, that it begins an atomic batch, and that no `SENDER` frame lies outside that batch. Calls `APPROVE(APPROVE_PAYMENT)` to authorize payment.
```

pr_title: Update EIP-8141: note sponsor repayment reversibility and batch the repayment in Example 3
author: svlachakis
body:
```suggestion
Note: payment collected at `APPROVE(APPROVE_PAYMENT)` in frame 1 is final and is not reverted by a later frame. Because every `SENDER` frame is inside the atomic batch begun by the repayment, a sponsee that zeroes its ERC-20 balance only causes its own intended call to be skipped and gains nothing; the sponsor still pays gas for the reverted attempt, which is the residual, unprofitable griefing risk inherent to public sponsorship.
```

pr_title: Update EIP-8141: note sponsor repayment reversibility and batch the repayment in Example 3
author: svlachakis
body:
```suggestion
Payment collected when a frame calls `APPROVE(APPROVE_PAYMENT)` or `APPROVE(APPROVE_EXECUTION_AND_PAYMENT)` is not reverted by the failure of any later frame. A frame that repays a sponsor (for example, an ERC-20 transfer to the sponsor) executing after payment approval is an ordinary frame: if it is not part of an atomic batch, its revert discards only that frame while the remaining frames, including the sponsee's intended operation, continue. A sponsee could therefore let the repayment frame revert while its intended operation still executes, obtaining execution without paying the sponsor. Sponsors should place the repayment frame and the sponsee's intended `SENDER` frame(s) in the same atomic batch so that they share fate, as shown in Example 3. The check must cover the whole frame list: the repayment frame begins an atomic batch and no `SENDER` frame lies outside it. A `SENDER` frame placed before the repayment or after the batch's terminal frame executes regardless of the repayment's fate. A `VERIFY` frame can perform this scan with `FRAMEPARAM` (mode and flags of every frame) before calling `APPROVE(APPROVE_PAYMENT)`. Only the gas payment itself is guaranteed final; all repayment and other post-payment effects are reversible.
```

pr_title: Update EIP-8141: note sponsor repayment reversibility and batch the repayment in Example 3
author: svlachakis
body:
I think "gains nothing" isn't true as stated. The check described (next frame is the repayment and it shares a batch with the intended call) is beatable:

| Frame | Mode | Flags |
|---|---|---|
| 2 | SENDER | ATOMIC_BATCH_FLAG (repayment) |
| 3 | SENDER | none (dummy, terminates the batch) |
| 4 | SENDER | none (real operation, outside the batch) |

Sponsee zeroes its balance → frame 2 reverts → batch [2,3] unrolls → frame 4 executes anyway, on the sponsor's gas. Placing the real operation before the repayment works too. The check that closes this: the repayment frame begins an atomic batch and no `SENDER` frame exists outside it. Suggestions inline.

Also, "payment is final and is not reverted by a later frame" is what [#11955](https://github.com/ethereum/EIPs/pull/11955) adds. Maybe merge that first or reference it, otherwise this note asserts something the spec text doesn't say yet.

pr_title: Update EIP-8141: approval effects are not reverted by frame revert or atomic-batch unroll
author: AnkushinDaniil
body:
Thanks, this is cleaner - agreed on both.

The effects-by-scope list duplicates the `APPROVE` section, so I'll drop it. And disallowing VERIFY frames in atomic batches removes the problem structurally: payment-`APPROVE` only happens in a VERIFY frame, so if VERIFY can't be batched, the payment is always collected before any SENDER batch and survives later SENDER-frame reverts by ordinary semantics - no transaction-scoped-survival wording or snapshot warning needed.

For context on why this came up: we hit the in-batch `APPROVE_PAYMENT` case in the Nethermind prototype - a snapshot-based batch rollback silently reverted the payer debit and nonce while `payer` survived, so the tx passed the `payer != None` check and the end refund paid uncollected funds. Forbidding VERIFY-in-batch is a simpler fix than exempting those writes, and it also covers what #11956 relies on.

So I'd restructure this PR to: (1) add a structural rule that a VERIFY frame MUST NOT be a member of an atomic batch (generalizing the mempool rule that already bans `ATOMIC_BATCH_FLAG` in the validation prefix); (2) take your rule 7 suggestion; (3) drop the effects re-list and the survival/snapshot paragraphs. One question - scope the rule to VERIFY frames, or more precisely any frame that calls `APPROVE`? Either works; VERIFY is where payment-approval lives.

Does that match what you had in mind? I'll push it if so.

pr_title: Update EIP-8141: specify EIP-3529 storage refund accounting for frames
author: lightclient
body:
> Per transaction breaks frame isolation: a refund earned in a cheap validation frame can subsidize an expensive later frame, so the accounting no longer matches "unused gas is not shared".

Should cost the same in validation and in later frames since pricing is at the tx level.

I think I'd prefer to do it on a per transaction basis. Keeping a global refund counter doesn't break the per frame isolation and I'm not sure if frames having a "net cost computable on [their] own" is all that useful.

Could be convinced otherwise if there are stronger reasons.

pr_title: Update EIP-8141: specify EIP-3529 storage refund accounting for frames
author: svlachakis
body:
> > Per transaction breaks frame isolation: a refund earned in a cheap validation frame can subsidize an expensive later frame, so the accounting no longer matches "unused gas is not shared".
> 
> Should cost the same in validation and in later frames since pricing is at the tx level.
> 
> I think I'd prefer to do it on a per transaction basis. Keeping a global refund counter doesn't break the per frame isolation and I'm not sure if frames having a "net cost computable on [their] own" is all that useful.
> 
> Could be convinced otherwise if there are stronger reasons.

@lightclient  Sounds good, the per-frame version was the conservative reading, but you're right that the gas limits stay per-frame either way and a single counter is what every client already implements. Updated the PR to specify the transaction-level counter with the one-fifth cap on total gas used.

pr_title: Update EIP-8141: specify EIP-3529 storage refund accounting for frames
author: soispoke
body:
The transaction refund accounting looks right, but the current text still leaves consensus details undefined.

Please specify:

- the EIP-3529 cap is computed from transaction gas used before the refund;
- changes to the refund counter from a reverted frame or rolled back atomic batch are discarded;
- `applied_refund = min(refund_counter, pre_refund_gas_used // 5)`; and
- gas before and after the refund use distinct names.

Each frame receipt should report gross gas before the refund because a transaction refund cannot be assigned uniquely to one frame.

pr_title: Update EIP-8141: specify EIP-3529 storage refund accounting for frames
author: svlachakis
body: @soispoke All good points, updated. The cap is now explicitly computed on `gross_gas_used` (pre-refund), counter changes from a reverted frame or unrolled batch are discarded with that frame's state, the formula is spelled out as `applied_refund = min(refund_counter, gross_gas_used // 5)`, and the two totals have distinct names. Frame receipts report gross gas per frame, since the transaction-level refund can't be attributed to any single frame.

pr_title: Update EIP-8141: specify EIP-3529 storage refund accounting for frames
author: AnkushinDaniil
body: I think the single tx-scoped refund counter with revert/batch discard is the right approach. One thing on the cap: `gross_gas_used` is frames-only, but 3529 caps at the whole tx pre-refund gas (intrinsic + calldata included). So a frame tx would get a smaller refund cap than the equivalent standard tx, which changes `total_gas_used` and the payer charge. Could we either use the full pre-refund charged gas, or say explicitly that it is a stricter frames-only base? Also a small clarification - is `cumulative_gas_used` net (post-refund) while the per-frame `gas_used` is gross? Might be worth one sentence since they will not sum

pr_title: Add EIP: Partial Execution Payload Commitments
author: jochem-brouwer
body:
RFC 2119 should only be used in Specifications: 


```suggestion
A malicious builder can sign several envelopes for the same bid that differ only in `state_root` and `block_hash`. All of them pass gossip validation, but at most one is execution valid. The first-seen gossip rule keeps honest nodes from forwarding more than one, yet an invalid envelope seen first can delay the valid one. Clients should drop envelopes that fail execution layer verification from their seen cache and accept a later envelope for the same `(beacon_block_root, builder_index)`. The equivocation is attributable, since it produces two signed envelopes for one beacon block root, and a slashing condition could be added. This matches the equivocation discussion in EIP-7732.
```

Otherwise, this could spec details which are not in the expect

pr_title: Add EIP: Partial Execution Payload Commitments
author: jochem-brouwer
body:
```suggestion
Under [EIP-7732's](./eip-7732.md) enshrined Proposer-Builder Separation (ePBS), a builder bid commits to the payload's `block_hash` and therefore to its `state_root`. This EIP makes the commitment partial: the bid fixes all payload contents except the `state_root` and the `block_hash` that depends on it. The full payload, including its state root, is still revealed in the `ExecutionPayloadEnvelope` and validated as today. Builders and provers gain the whole window between bid and reveal to compute the state root, instead of needing one for every candidate bid. Execution layer state root semantics do not change.
```

pr_title: Update EIP-8141: bound the signatures list with MAX_SIGNATURES
author: svlachakis
body:
> I would lean to not cap the signature list size, since it is already capped by the gas limit.

@lightclient Fair for the priced schemes, but I think `ARBITRARY` entries break the argument: `signature_gas` is 0 and empty signer/msg/signature fields have zero calldata cost, so `[0x0, empty, empty, empty] `adds nothing to `tx_gas_limit`. That's ~5 RLP bytes per entry ~26k entries in a 128KB tx and all of it is decode work done before any gas check can reject, with no per-entry cost to bail against. That's what pushed me to an explicit bound; it's also most probably why `MAX_FRAMES` exists even though frames cost 475 each.

```suggestion
*Valid* code has fully static control flow: every transfer of control lands where the code says it does.  Validation does at `CREATE` time what `JUMPDEST` analysis does at run time, and proves more: the destination of every jump and call, that every return has a call to return from, that within each subroutine the depth of the *data stack* at every instruction is the same on every execution, and that no instruction can find fewer items than it removes.
```

body:
```suggestion
Execution is defined in the [Yellow Paper](https://github.com/ethereum/yellowpaper/blob/f15fa703d03d6ae31cf99034cacc621146fda1c7/paper.pdf) as a sequence of changes to the EVM state.  Exceptional halting conditions are properties of the machine state, checked before each instruction executes: if executing would violate one, execution halts instead — as the Yellow Paper puts it (§9.4.2), "no instruction can, through its execution, cause an exceptional halt."  Proving that no reachable state violates a condition therefore proves that no execution can reach an exceptional halting state.  That is what validation does — once, at `CREATE` time.  The Yellow Paper defines six conditions:
```

pr_title: Update EIP-8037: apply the EIP-7976 calldata floor to block-level gas accounting
author: Helkomine
body:
> The principle: the floor prices calldata, a regular-dimension resource; state gas prices trie growth, a different resource. Each dimension's bound must be satisfied by that dimension alone — letting state gas satisfy the calldata floor reopens the block-size hole of Section 1 for anyone willing to buy some storage slots alongside their data. (The _sender-side_ formula intentionally keeps the transaction-total comparison `max(used, F)`, so users are not double-charged; only block accounting is per-dimension.)

I'm not sure what this section means. Didn't it already perform a pre-transaction check where `max(intrinsic_gas, calldata_floor_gas_cost) <= TX_MAX_GAS_LIMIT`, and that calldata floor filling other resources was already allowed in 7623?

pr_title: Update EIP-8037: apply the EIP-7976 calldata floor to block-level gas accounting
author: jochem-brouwer
body:
I have updated the post @Helkomine. The section described that we have two gas dimensions, regular and state gas. In the current `master` version of the EIP we have for block accounting:

`tx_regular_gas = tx_gas_used_after_refund - tx_state_gas`

```
tx_gas_used_before_refund = tx.gas - tx_output.gas_left - tx_output.state_gas_reservoir
tx_gas_refund = min(tx_gas_used_before_refund // 5, tx_output.refund_counter)
tx_gas_used_after_refund = tx_gas_used_before_refund - tx_gas_refund
```

(Note that the calldata floor is not part of any of these formulas). The point is that EIP-7623 (see Rationale) attempts to limit the max block size, which should thus be accounted for. Since currently the calldata floor is not part of the block accounting formula, this seems incorrect to me. Since the gas used of a block MUST be equal to or lower than the block gas limit, we can thus use that as a cap: since we use the maximum of the regular and state gas used, we should thus ensure that at least one of them adds at least the calldata floor gas to the block accounting: if we do that, then the block is bounded by the calldata. After taking this maximum, no subtractions should happen, as this is essentially a "discount on the floor price". We must ensure that the floor gas cost propagates through at least one of the gas dimensions.

If this is not what you meant then happily explain further :smile: :+1:

pr_title: Update EIP-8037: apply the EIP-7976 calldata floor to block-level gas accounting
author: Helkomine
body: Thank you, now I understand. Perhaps I misunderstood the interpretation of block level -> transaction level

pr_title: Update EIP-8037: apply the EIP-7976 calldata floor to block-level gas accounting
author: Helkomine
body: Although this is unrelated, I think we can abstract away the impact of EIP-2780. EIP-8037 only defines the state creation fee, EIP-8038 only defines the state access fee, and EIP-2780 uses these definitions in its intrinsic fee accounting, which allows for the elimination of circular dependencies between different EIPs, something we want to avoid.

pr_title: Update EIP-8311: Apply refund for calldata floor gas
author: Helkomine
body:
I'm concerned that further increases in calldata costs and adds of content floor will begin to impact users beyond the "minimal" impact it previously had, so I want to add a reasonable discount to somewhat mitigate this impact

If the goal of this EIP is to align it with the transaction envelope, then I think that should be applied at the block level and the impact of EIP-7976 should remain at the transaction level as it is now. I think this approach would be more appropriate than a refund since we also have EIP-7778

pr_title: Update EIP-8311: Apply refund for calldata floor gas

There are only so few transactions impacted and I doubt that receiving a refund for SSTOREs while hitting the floor would give us anything. Also, it's impact on users is a different concern (assuming refunds change nothing), but one to be taken seriously ofc. I did look into the impact of this change and remember it was rather minimal, but def higher with 7976, and accounting for 8131 and 8279.

pr_title: Update EIP-8311: Apply refund for calldata floor gas
author: Helkomine
body:
Thank you for your comment. A refund might not be a reasonable solution, but what do you think if we instead maintain the 64/64 floor on transactions and apply 96/96 at the block level?
I don't have the resources to statistic how many transactions are affected, but I have randomly observed several 4337 transactions and noticed that they are more likely to be affected quite frequently when applying the 8131+8279+8311 trio because they carry a significant amount of calldata (userop) and also contain a lot of cold access

body:
This slightly contradicts EIP-7928 as it currently stands. It says
"Transaction sender and recipient addresses (even for zero-value transfers)" MUST be included in the BAL.

If we include the recipient at this stage, the BAL for a transaction which OOGs at the auth processing will not have the recipient (in contradiction to EIP-7928).

pr_title: Update EIP-2780: clarify 2780
author: gurukamath
body:
It may just be an issue with how I am reading it. The way it is currently structured, it seems to say

```
Then the recipient account is added to the BAL and unless the transaction is a self-transfer or a contract creation:

- if the recipient is non-existent and tx.value > 0, charge STATE_BYTES_PER_NEW_ACCOUNT × CPSB in state gas;
- if the recipient is an [EIP-7702](https://github.com/rjl493456442/EIPs/blob/2780-clarify/EIPS/eip-7702.md) delegated account, additionally charge the delegation-target access in regular gas — COLD_ACCOUNT_ACCESS if cold, WARM_ACCESS if warm.
```

Which makes me think the 2 charges should not apply if it is a self transfer. In any case, this is very minor

pr_title: Update EIP-2780: clarify 2780
author: misilva73
body:
TX_VALUE_COST was derived in two steps:
- First, we take the diff between the cost of a transfer without value (15k) and a transfer with value (21k). This is based on [benchmarks](https://misilva73.github.io/eip-2780-repricing/index.html). Note that Erigon is still working on their optimizations, so I am taking the 2nd worst client for now.
- To this diff, we remove the log cost - this cost covers mostly history growth, so the execution cost is orthogonal.

pr_title: Update EIP-7778: Move to Review
author: jochem-brouwer
body:
LGTM!

@nerolation @benaadams want to flag some things what likely should be addressed:

> - Storage discounts that reflect actual reduced computational work (e.g., warm storage access, reverting to original values) remain applied to block gas accounting

Reverting to original values per [EIP-2200](https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-2200#specification) adds to refund counter, so does or does this not get subtracted from the block accounting? It seems to me that we ban all refunds from the block accounting (not from tx accounting)? I think the original assumption was that the revert to original values gets a discount, but it actually gets a refund, so that example should be removed from this bullet point.

### Receipt semantics

EIP states:

>  Transaction gas: `gas_spent = max(tx_gas_used - gas_refund, calldata_floor_gas_cost)`

For clarity it should also state that cumulative gas used (in the receipt) is thus this value, and not the value used for block accounting.

pr_title: Add EIP: Align Checkpoint with Epoch Boundary Block
author: lodekeeper
body:
Reviewed as a listed co-author and from the Lodestar/consensus side — approving. I re-derived the changes against current `consensus-specs` rather than taking them at face value.

**Accessor + call sites.** `get_checkpoint_root(state, epoch)` → `get_block_root_at_slot(state, compute_start_slot_at_epoch(epoch) - 1)` (genesis → `GENESIS_SLOT`) is the correct "last block before the epoch." The three substitutions land on the right functions: `get_attestation_participation_flag_indices` (matching-target, today `get_block_root(state, data.target.epoch)`), `weigh_justification_and_finalization` (the recorded checkpoint `root`), and fork choice `get_checkpoint_block` (today `get_ancestor(..., compute_start_slot_at_epoch(epoch))`). Source/head matching, justification bits, and finalization rules are correctly left untouched.

**Checkpoint state is invariant — the part I most wanted to confirm.** `store_target_checkpoint_state` already does `if base_state.slot < compute_start_slot_at_epoch(target.epoch): process_slots(...)`. Under the new anchoring `target.root` is the boundary block (slot < epoch start), so that `process_slots` path runs and yields the *same* checkpoint state as today. This isn't new code — it's already exercised whenever an epoch's first slot is empty, which is exactly why "make the fallback the rule" is minimally invasive. No change to checkpoint-state handling is needed, and the EIP correctly omits one.

**Removing the honest-validator first-slot special case is enabled, not just cosmetic.** That special case existed because `get_block_root(head_state, N)` in the first slot resolves to `get_block_root_at_slot(state, state.slot)`, which violates the `slot < state.slot` bound. `get_checkpoint_root` reads slot `start-1 < state.slot`, so the boundary case disappears and the special-casing can go.

**Fork transition is the sharp edge and it's handled correctly.** Resolving pre-activation epochs under the *old* anchoring is required, not optional: `filter_block_tree`'s finalized-root match and the ~1-epoch tail of still-includable pre-activation attestations both break if the finalized/target epoch is re-resolved under the new rule before a post-activation checkpoint finalizes. Good that the Specification pins this to `epoch < activation`.

Editorial: abcoathup's and jochem-brouwer's inline comments are all addressed and the threads resolved on `22a8944b` (FFG expanded, function provenance stated, test-cases intro added, filename/number, discussions-to). @jochem-brouwer's `CHANGES_REQUESTED` was from `3d5cfefd` and looks stale — worth a re-review to clear it. CI is green on head; the earlier github-actions failure was on the superseded `3d5cfefd`.

Overall a clean framing: same epochs, same containers, same slashing/finality math — only the block a checkpoint names moves, from a redundant first-slot block to the boundary block that actually determines the epoch's start state.

author: auryn-macmillan
body: I've been wondering why Ethereum doesn't use drand-like timelock encryption for prevrandao?

pr_title: Add EIP: Hash-Chain RANDAO
author: TomWambsgans
body:
I am curious: why not removing the ability to update the commitment? (as a simplification)
Rationale: a standard CPU core can compute > 10^7 sha2 / s. Even at 1 chain reveal per second, a pre-computation of 10 min would last 190 years. (10^7 * 60 * 10 / (3600 * 24 * 365) = 190). To solve storage issue, we could just store one chain value every 10^6.

pr_title: Add EIP: Hash-Chain RANDAO
author: kevaundray
body:
> I am curious: why not removing the ability to update the commitment? (as a simplification) Rationale: a standard CPU core can compute > 10^7 sha2 / s. Even at 1 chain reveal per second, a pre-computation of 10 min would last 190 years. (10^7 * 60 * 10 / (3600 * 24 * 365) = 190). To solve storage issue, we could just store one chain value every 10^6.

Thats a good point on lifetimes; since a chain reveal happens on every proposal (which is not that often for most validators, we can even say 100 proposals a year), 10^7 would likely never need to be renewed ever.

If we remove the ability to change the commitment, then I think the following would change:

- We still have a commitment change message, since we want users to be able to update from bls to hash-chain

   This can only be removed if we allow users to register the hash chain commitment when they deposit, but would require deeper changes

- The commitment change message is only valid if the previous commitment value was zero; ie the user has not registered a hash-chain commitment yet

- If a user wants to change their hash chain commitment, then they will need to exit and enter again

This doesn't require us to change exit logic because validator indices are always increasing right now, and the commitment is linked to a validator's index 

- We _may_ still need to have the commitment change epoch delay because a validator may choose to grind and register their hash chain just before they are about to propose. They can only do this attack once though, unless they exit and enter to redo it, but this seems unrealistic

pr_title: Add EIP: Hash-Chain RANDAO
author: kevaundray
body:
Right now, if you lose the component that is responsible for RANDAO (ie your BLS private key) you have effectively lost your validator. 

In that sense, @TomWambsgans I think your suggestion to only allow registering but not updating makes sense, and users will need to treat their hash-chain commitment/seed like they would treat their bls secret (ensuring it is correctly generated etc)

pr_title: Add EIP: Hash-Chain RANDAO
author: b-wagn
body:
For this application, I think preimage resistance is not enough, we need collision-resistance.

For instance, if I can find a collision or multi-collision (say `H(x_i) = H(x_0)` for all `i`), then I just build my hash chain so that involves this collision, e.g., start from `x_0`. Once I need to reveal my next preimage, I can still decide if I reveal `x_0` or `x_1` or ... . So I get bias. This is exactly why we required the uniqueness of BLS. Here, collision resistance gives you some form of computational uniqueness.

body: A collision, see above.

pr_title: Add EIP: Hash-Chain RANDAO
author: b-wagn
body: Maybe we should say something here already about the "bounded length" drawback of this solution (which is not a big drawback in my opinion). With BLS / unique signatures, your pk serves as a commitment that has unlimited lifetime. Here, the lifetime is given by the length of the chain. We make a similar compromise for XMSS, and it is ok if the lifetime is huge, e.g., hash chain of length `2^20` or something.

pr_title: Add EIP: Hash-Chain RANDAO
author: jochem-brouwer
body:
```suggestion
Replace the BLS-signature-based Random Decentralized Autonomous Organization (RANDAO) reveal with a hash-chain commit-reveal scheme. RANDAO's resistance to grinding currently relies on BLS signatures being *unique*, so that a proposer cannot bias its contribution. Since BLS relies on pre-quantum hardness assumptions, a quantum computer can recover a validator's key and predict its future reveals.
```

pr_title: Add EIP: Hash-Chain RANDAO
author: GottfriedHerold
body: I might be worth mentioning that not only can the attacker predict the schedule in advance, but it can also influence it (much better than without a CRQC): The standard reveal-or-not attack usually requires the attacker to have $k$ consecutive proposer slots at the end of an epoch to choose from $2^k$ options. If the attacker can predict others' randomness contributions, they can now user any $k$ slots (assuming all honest parties always reveal) ; they do not need to be consecutive or at the end of an epoch.

author: tcoratger
body:
"MAY" should be capital letter no?

```suggestion
No chain value MAY be the zero word: `process_randao` rejects a zero reveal (the zero word marks an unregistered validator), and a zero commitment cannot be registered. The seed `c_0` is chosen non-zero, and every other `c_i` is a SHA-256 output, so a zero link occurs only with negligible probability (about `n / 2**256`). Even so, a validator MUST check that no `c_i` is the zero word and regenerate the chain if any link is zero.
```

pr_title: Add EIP: Hash-Chain RANDAO
author: tcoratger
body:
I imagine that the recommendation will be made to the client teams to have a large enough `n`. But since the fact of having to exit the validator set and re-enter it is very painful, can't we have a sort of delayed commitment rotation?

I think this adds a bit of complexity but basically what we could do is to allow a validator to register a replacement hash chain before the current one is exhausted.

For example when the validator has, say, 1,000 links left, it generates another chain and submits a fresh `RandaoCommitmentRotation` signed by its validator signing key. The protocol does not activate `d_m` immediately. It places it in a pending queue and activates it after the same safe lookahead delay used for initial registration:

```
activation_epoch = inclusion_epoch + COMMITMENT_REGISTRATION_DELAY
```

pr_title: Add EIP: Hash-Chain RANDAO
author: jochem-brouwer
body:
```suggestion
Most uses of signatures, such as block proposals and attestations, can move to any secure post-quantum scheme. RANDAO, however, additionally depends on signature *uniqueness*, and most post-quantum schemes do not provide it, allowing one to grind for a favorable RANDAO contribution. The lean signature scheme currently planned for the consensus layer is grindable in exactly this way, since it includes a *salt* component.
```

pr_title: Add EIP: Hash-Chain RANDAO
author: jochem-brouwer
body:
```suggestion
This EIP requires a scheduled consensus-layer hard fork. Within the fork, the change is backwards compatible from the validator's perspective: unregistered validators continue proposing exactly as today. Downstream consumers of `randao_mixes` (including the execution layer's [EIP-4399's](./eip-4399.md) `PREVRANDAO`) are unaffected; the mix remains a 32-byte accumulator updated once per block, only the provenance of contributions changes.
```

pr_title: Update EIP-7997: Add EAS-like bytecode + add required EIP
author: jochem-brouwer
body:
EIP-161 is implicitly required because of the hard-enforcement of setting nonce to 1 for the irregular state transition (or at least the result enforces that once the contract is deployed it has nonzero nonce). I assume this is because otherwise, if the nonce is not changed, it could deploy a contract with nonce 0, which would then be a new-ish kind of account which cannot be deployed anymore currently.

Note that prior to EIP-161 (Spurious Dragon) contracts deployed had nonce 0, and those which do not have CREATE/CALLCODE/DELEGATECALL opcodes are (currently) not possible to raise their nonce, so an account of type: "has code, nonce zero" currently exist on Mainnet.

I am actually not sure if we should impose "rules" in this EIP for the state transition. I would argue to simplify this EIP we leave out the irregular state transition in the specification. This EIP, once it is active, enforces that this specific address has this specific bytecode, and nothing more.

If a chain cannot deploy the factory by the keyless transaction and it did not have it in genesis, then this chain itself should come up with a way to add this factory (likely: via an irregular state transition).

Moving the Upgrade Meta EIP to `Review` at the beginning of the devnet phase gives client teams, enterprises, and the broader community sufficient time to thoroughly review the upgrade while signaling that the proposal has reached a more stable stage than `Draft`, encouraging more focused feedback.

pr_title: Update EIP-7773: Move to Review
author: poojaranjan
body:
@jochem-brouwer 

Upon further consideration, it makes sense to remove the `Proposed for Inclusion` list alongside `Declined for Inclusion` when the Upgrade Meta EIP is promoted to `Review` status.
 
#### Why should `Proposed for Inclusion` be removed when the Upgrade Meta EIP is promoted to `Review`?

Ideally, an Upgrade Meta EIP should only be promoted to `Review` once all EIPs referenced in the proposal - regardless of their Upgrade Stage have reached at least `Review` status. In practice, by this point all candidate EIPs will already be undergoing testing on either EIP or upgrade devnets, meaning the window for proposing additional EIPs has effectively closed. As a result, the `Proposed for Inclusion` list no longer serves a meaningful purpose and instead becomes a blocker to promoting the Meta EIP.

Additionally, similar to `Declined for Inclusion`, there is a high likelihood that the `Proposed for Inclusion` list will contain at least one EIP that is still in `Draft` status. Since the repository bot prevents a Meta EIP from being merged while it references a `Draft' EIP, these entries must be removed before the Meta EIP can progress.

For these reasons, I propose removing both the `Proposed for Inclusion` and `Declined for Inclusion` lists when the Upgrade Meta EIP is promoted to `Review`, leaving only the sections that remain relevant for the rest of the upgrade lifecycle.

----
`When the Upgrade Meta EIP is moved to `Review`, the `Proposed for Inclusion` and `Declined for Inclusion` list **SHOULD** be removed. When it is moved to `Last Call`, the `Considered for Inclusion` lists **SHOULD** be removed, leaving only the `Scheduled for Inclusion` list.`

> why the urgency to move it to Review when there are still open PFIs and the fork is still actively being adjusted? 

I agree that it’s best to move the Meta EIP to `Review` once we clean up the PFI/CFI/DFI sections. 

From the last ACD meetings, it appears Glamsterdam is entering to Devnet 7 and within weeks to the Public testnet.

> This doesn't follow precedent and I don't see a benefit to moving it right now - Fusaka was https://github.com/ethereum/EIPs/pull/10337 about 6 weeks before going live.

For Standards track Core EIPs, [status transition could be tied to the network upgrade stage](https://github.com/ethereum/EIPs/pull/11855#issuecomment-4872040005) rather than a fixed number of calendar weeks before mainnet. This is an effort to create a precedent.

pr_title: Update EIP-2780: move state-dependent charges to runtime (cold surcharge, new-account state gas)
author: jochem-brouwer
body:
(this is an edited post after Claude posted this without my permission :sweat_smile: It now reflects my thoughts)

The EIP-7702 authorization gas rules are now specified in three places, in two incompatible models:

- **This PR**: `REGULAR_PER_AUTH_BASE_COST` at the intrinsic phase, plus conditional runtime charges (new-account state gas, `ACCOUNT_WRITE`, delegation-indicator bytes), with no refills.
- **EIP-8037**, "Gas accounting for EIP-7702 authorizations": worst-case intrinsic charge (`ACCOUNT_WRITE` + `(STATE_BYTES_PER_NEW_ACCOUNT + STATE_BYTES_PER_AUTH_BASE) × CPSB` per authorization) corrected by refill rules 1–3 during authorization processing.
- **EIP-8038**, "EIP-7702 authorizations pricing": its own table restating the worst-case intrinsic model.

Related: this PR states *"the per-authority rules of EIP-8037 ensure each charge below is applied at most once per authority"* — but those rules are refill rules for the worst-case-intrinsic model and do not directly translate to the conditional-charge model used here (e.g. the `0->a->0->a` pattern I [asked](https://github.com/ethereum/EIPs/pull/11844#discussion_r3518940394) about above needs explicit rules in the conditional model, since there is no worst-case charge to refill against).

I checked the open PRs against EIP-8037/EIP-8038 and none reconciles this; #11778 even builds further on the worst-case refill model, and #11826 keeps the EIP-8038 authorizations table. We should decide which EIP owns transaction-level authorization charging. If it moves here, which I think would make sense (this EIP "owns" the newly introduced "topmost frame", which is now not the frame which defines all pre-execution logic (state creation costs, EIP-7702 delegations) at the transaction level) then EIP-8037 and EIP-8038 need corresponding PRs removing or deferring their versions, and EIP-8037's reservoir initialization (`intrinsic_state_gas`) has to be restated for the case where no state gas is charged intrinsically.

**This also means that we would have to enforce some kind of EIP-dependency tree** so we can walk "down" the tree to figure out where the root rules can be found (a rule should only be stated once, and should not have a "copy" of the rule: EIPs should link to the definition to the specific EIP, without quoting it, to ensure there are no conflicting rules)

author: misilva73
body:
```suggestion
The gas charing is split across two phases. **Intrinsic gas** is the state-independent cost of including the transaction in a block and is the sole input to the transaction-validity check. **Runtime gas** covers the state-dependent charges — the recipient cold surcharge, new-account creation, and delegation resolution - charged as the first frame is entered, metered in same way as inside the frame. Running out of gas in runtime does not invalidate the transaction. Instead, the transaction is included, execution is skipped, and all state changes are reverted, as for any out-of-gas halt inside a frame.
```

pr_title: Update EIP-2780: move state-dependent charges to runtime (cold surcharge, new-account state gas)
author: jochem-brouwer
body:
If I understand it correctly I think we can simplify this change.

```suggestion
The gas charging is split across two phases. **Intrinsic gas** is the state-independent cost of including the transaction in a block and is the sole input to the transaction-validity check. **Runtime gas** covers the state-dependent charges — the recipient cold surcharge, new-account creation, and delegation resolution - charged as the first frame is entered from their respective gas dimension. In case that the transaction cannot pay for these costs, all the remaining gas is consumed and all state changes are reverted.
```

> all state changes are reverted

is somewhat confusing, because the account nonce and the account balance (+coinbase balance if tx has priority fee) always changes, so that obviously should not be reverted.

The current text says: 

> as for any out-of-gas halt inside a frame.

This is not true, if the execution part of the tx OOGs currently, then all state changes in execution are rolled back, but the EIP-7702 delegations still persist. In this situation (insufficient gas to pay for all the state changes) it is different, as prior to entering the first frame we already OOG. 

Currently (Osaka) the state creation gas for EIP-7702 authorizations is guaranteed to exist because it comes from the 25k intrinsic cost of a EIP-7702 transaction (get a refund if the account exists). However, now once we enter the frame we start charging state gas costs and also regular gas costs. The question is: in which order is this charged? What if we can pay state gas for a few EIP-7702 authorizations, but for others not? Do we rollback all authorizations we just made? Or do we keep those we can pay for and then OOG? This should be addressed. In case that we keep the ones we can pay for then it must be made clear in what specific order these gas costs are deducted, as this in some situations influences if an authorization could be paid for or not.

> On an exceptional halt the same refill applies, but `gas_left` is consumed, so only the reservoir portion survives.

It confuses me.

For example, if we have a contract creation transaction, and the top-level create frame halts (e.g. due to an address collision). Should we also burn the transaction's remaining regular gas after applying the LIFO refunds?

For comparison, for `CREATE/CREATE2`, if the child create frame halts, we:

- revert its state changes and refund the child frame's state cost via LIFO (resetting the child's reservoir back to its original value);
- refund the parent frame's state cost via LIFO.

The parent frame then continues execution normally; it is not itself considered halted.

My question is whether a top-level contract creation transaction should behave differently. Should the top-most frame also preserve its remaining regular gas after the LIFO refunds, or should the halt be treated as propagating to the top level, causing the remaining regular gas to be burned as a special case?

cc @misilva73

author: jochem-brouwer
body:
I did review up to but not including the test cases.

I get the idea, but this is extremely complex and the test cases here are exploding. We have the BAL interactions which depend on "when" a state is read, we have changes to EIP-7702 intrinsic gas costs, we seem to have a change in behavior of EIP-7702 delegations in case the pre-execution gas OOGs, it seems we can OOG but get a refund (?), we also have the interactions with the floor gas - is all the gas consumed as execution gas (I assume so, but this should be declared). There are also the interactions with EIP-2930 tx access lists.

For the EIP-7702 situation: the original idea was that we pay the 25k intrinsic to ensure that the gas to create an account is paid upfront. One gets 12.5k back if the account already exists. Why don't we do this here also? The intrinsic gas cost of EIP-7702 now covers the situation where we have to delegate a new account. Once we are charging this gas and see the account already exists, then the state gas is refunded to the reservoir.

I feel like this idea can be written down a bit more simple, for instance by explaining the execution costs (also in which order) for the CREATE- and CALL- like situations.
