pr_title: Update EIP-7999: add data and state resources, simplify gas accounting
author: anderselowsson
body:
Thanks for the PR!

Concerning having no limit for state. The potential downside is that someone can buy big chunks of state in a single tx/block at a fixed price. At the same time, there are benefits from a CR perspective (FOCIL inclusion check). A high limit such as 32x can also provide good CR, but of course no limits excludes state completely from any issues there. Can we quantify the implicit limits due to coupling with other resources, and take it from there?

Using the 120 GiB/year target (~49 kB per block) from EIP-8037, and a 600M execution gas limit, I get the following target/limit ratios:

- including EIP-7702 authorizations to empty accounts: `12,041` execution gas for `143` state bytes, i.e. 145x the state target?
- excluding EIP-7702 authorizations: value-bearing `CALL` to a non-existent account gives `11,000` execution gas for `120` state bytes, i.e. 133x the state target?
- `SSTORE` zero-to-nonzero gives `13,000` execution gas for `64` state bytes, i.e. 60x the state target?

The outcome will then drift with the execution gas limit. Does it make sense? And then for contract creation we instead need to compare with the data resource. For max-size contracts, there is roughly 1-to-1 in terms of bytes. So at a 6MB data limit that is about 123x the state target. Empty contracts are `120` state bytes per `28` data bytes, so as a data-only bound, assuming enough execution gas, at a 6MB data limit that gives about 525x the state target? I see the PR put the implicit data limit a little lower though.

EIP-7999 would seem like a possible opportunity to move away from gas units by the way. We could clean up by going to bytes directly, although I appreciate there may be complexities associated with this.

The second point is about setting transaction resource limits. As previously discussed and you also have noted, the idea behind 7999 is to have separate resource limits indicated by the user as we move into the EVM. We then pursue universal overflow for facilitating subcalls. This means that we would have to move away from the state gas reservoir in its present form, so it should not be adopted. Specifically, we are not pursuing "Aggregate EVM gas" as defined in the EIP spec for the baseline implementation.

author: benaadams

> * Rename the file to `Remove the Refund Mechanism`.
> * Officially removing transaction-level refund (which also impacts block-level) aims to simplify the implementation but does not significantly affect users.

It isn't removing the refund mechanism?

pr_title: Update EIP-7778: Block Gas Accounting without Refunds and Route Refunds
author: Helkomine
body: Yes, my intention is to remove the old refund counter (from EIP-3529) because it is creating too much complexity in the EIP-8038 implementation. The idea is to eliminate out-of-transaction refund sources (e.g., slot clearing) to optimize for internal refund accounting (e.g., `ACCOUNT_WRITE` refunds in EIP-8038). In terms of impact, I think this won't be too significant because transaction costs will become cheaper after Glamsterdam, and internal optimizations could make transactions even cheaper.

pr_title: Update EIP-7778: Block Gas Accounting without Refunds and Route Refunds
author: Helkomine
body: I changed the phrase to "remove old refund" to emphasize that only the old refund mechanism since EIP-3529 is being removed, while the new refund accounting models (e.g., the `state_gas_reservoir` of EIP-8037) are perfectly effective and are not within the scope of regulation.

pr_title: Update EIP-7778: Block Gas Accounting without Refunds and Route Refunds
author: nerolation
body:
Yeah I see the simplification argument, and I really like the pr for that. This has been discussed in an ACD when 7778 got cfi'd and by that time we decided to keep the refund as clearing state, in times when state is increasingly becoming a problem, is something we may want to keep.
I personally don't have a strong opinion but would also lean towards keeping it. With increasing state-access costs (EIP-8037, EIP-8038), the refund should increase too, and with state growth increasingly becoming a problem, refunds could be further incentiviced.

pr_title: Update EIP-7778: Block Gas Accounting without Refunds and Route Refunds
author: Helkomine
body: Actually, I didn't want to remove this refund feature, but I had to in order to add optimizations to the 8038. The 8038 contains complex processing when handling refunds for the 3529, and I want to replace it with a more efficient model similar to the 8037. I was concerned that adding too many refund mechanisms at once would slow down client workflows, so I decided to remove it to make way for more efficient refund accounting.

Would this necessarily come with dropping the 20% cap?
The refund mechanism has been quite stable and hasn't been touched in a while. I'd prefer not changing 7778 at this stage (it's been included in early devnets and has been fine for months now).

pr_title: Update EIP-7778: Block Gas Accounting without Refunds and Route Refunds
author: Helkomine
body: Yes, it might not be necessary. However, considering that EIP-8038 is handling complex cases related to slot deletion refunds, and it was recently discovered to have a bug in its `SSTORE` accounting method, I'm reconsidering removing the refund mechanism of EIP-3529. Perhaps we should keep this EIP and simply remove the `SSTORE` slot clearing refund; the refund counter will still exist, but it will no longer be meaningful. I will keep this PR until EIP-8038 is fully resolved.

pr_title: Add EIP: Post-Quantum Keystore for Stateful Keys
author: jochem-brouwer
body:
```suggestion
The key words "MUST", "MUST NOT", "REQUIRED", "SHOULD", "SHOULD NOT", and "MAY" in this document are to be interpreted as described in [RFC 2119](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2119) and [RFC 8174](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8174).
```

pr_title: Add EIP: Post-Quantum Keystore for Stateful Keys
author: jochem-brouwer
body:
```suggestion
This standard defines a keystore format for **stateful hash-based signing keys**, specifically eXtended Merkle Signature Scheme (XMSS) as used by the Lean Ethereum consensus layer (hereafter `leanxmss`). It extends [ERC-2335](./eip-2335.md) so that the encrypted secret may be an XMSS seed and adds the machinery a *consumable* key requires: an explicit scheme-parameter block, a non-authoritative capacity snapshot, normative rules for where the authoritative signing state lives, a commit-before-sign durability requirement, reserved leaf ranges for concurrent signers, and import/export semantics that forbid silently resetting a key's signing position.
```

Define abbreviations before use, and use Lean Ethereum (both capitalized) consistently.

From EIP-1:

pr_title: Add EIP: Post-Quantum Keystore for Stateful Keys
author: jochem-brouwer
body:
```suggestion
v5 is not backwards compatible with v4 consumers, which assume a reusable 32-byte secret and have no notion of state authority. v4 and v5 keystores are distinguished by the `version` field and the presence of the `scheme` object. A v5-aware client must refuse to operate on a consumable key as if it were a v4 reusable key. v4 BLS keystores remain valid under their own standard and are out of scope.
```

pr_title: Add EIP: Post-Quantum Keystore for Stateful Keys
author: jochem-brouwer
body:
```suggestion
- **Leaf reuse is catastrophic and silent.** Unlike a slashing event, reuse may produce no immediate on-chain penalty while fully compromising the key. The §4 ordering and §6 import rules are the primary defenses and must not be relaxed for performance.
```

pr_title: Add EIP: Post-Quantum Keystore for Stateful Keys
author: jochem-brouwer
body:
```suggestion
- **Stale-restore is the dominant operational risk.** Backups protect the seed but not the state. Operators MUST be guided toward recover-then-reconcile, never restore-and-sign. Detection of high-water regression (§6) is required.
```

pr_title: Add EIP: Post-Quantum Keystore for Stateful Keys
author: jochem-brouwer
body:
```suggestion
- **State store integrity.** An attacker able to roll back the authoritative state can induce reuse. The state store should have integrity protection commensurate with the keystore itself.
```

pr_title: Add EIP: Post-Quantum Keystore for Stateful Keys
author: jochem-brouwer
body:
```suggestion
- **Cloning across hosts.** Running the same key on two hosts without disjoint reserved ranges guarantees reuse. Range assignment (§5) must be exclusive.
```

pr_title: Update EIP-8141: Spec cleanup and clarifications
author: derekchiang
body:
I think the signature index thing is mostly an optimization for quantum (since the outer signatures can be aggregated and then removed from the txns), which is not really useful here since the signature is ECDSA.

Re why no P256 support -- supporting P256 in the default code means that we'd have to support P256-EOAs, where the EOA address is derived from P256 pub key.  My initial version of default code actually did support that, but after some discussions with @lightclient we decided to remove it since introducing a new class of passkey-derived EOAs may open a can of worms that is hard to put back.

pr_title: Update EIP-8141: Spec cleanup and clarifications
author: derekchiang
body:
By the way, another TODO for the default code is that we need to define a gas schedule for it.  Since the default code is implemented not in the EVM but rather in client code, it's not clear how much gas it costs, unless we define it.

Or, we could define the default code in terms of EVM bytecode.

pr_title: Update EIP-8141: Spec cleanup and clarifications
author: morph-dev
body:
I think signature index makes design cleaner. Why would code iterate over all signatures and try to check which one of them matches the requirements (scheme, msg, target), when we can just pass the index and it only checks one. Also, having index would make it easier to design gas schedule (if we want it to be executed as client code rather than EVM bytecode).

Regarding P256 support, I can see that as a good enough reason. It's something we can easily add in the future.

pr_title: Add EIP: Trustless log and transaction index
author: SamWilsn
body:
```suggestion
Full nodes can maintain their own index structures but most users rely on remote providers that cannot prove the correctness of the results of user queries. Relying on trusted sources for obtaining the output of smart contracts defeats the purpose of maintaining those contracts on a distributed trustless ledger. As the processing capacity of Ethereum grows, this information asymmetry just gets worse. Trustless provability throughout the entire stack, from end user applications signing transactions, to the same or other end user applications getting the results they need, should be part of the roadmap.
```

A bit too informal I think.

pr_title: Update EIP-8038: Add preliminary numbers
author: Helkomine
body: For some read-only operations from memory, such as `warm SLOAD`, should we charge a lower cost, similar to `MLOAD`? The 100 gas cost should only be applied to operations that may result in REVERT path processing, such as `warm SSTORE` and `warm CALL`.

pr_title: Update EIP-8038: Add preliminary numbers
author: Helkomine
body: Except for `STORAGE_CLEAR_REFUND`, all costs should be `refill` instead of `refund` because these costs originate from the transaction itself. Including them in a refund counter would render the gas inefficient, perhaps we should record them in a separate counter.

pr_title: Update EIP-8038: Add preliminary numbers
author: Helkomine
body:
I expect this to be the maximum value calculated for each transfer, while the final value will depend on whether the target account has been previously updated and the amount of gas it consumes.
Additionally, we should also consider refunds in cases where the balance update is in the pattern x -> y -> x.

pr_title: Update EIP-8038: Add preliminary numbers
author: Helkomine
body: If the target account have been previously written (a target account that complies with EIP-684 receives ether in the same transaction but before CREATE is executed), the expected cost is `CREATE_ACCESS - ACCOUNT_WRITE`

pr_title: Add EIP: SETCODEFROM Code Reuse Instruction
author: Helkomine
body:
There are issues with the design you proposed:

- Ineffective coverage: EIP-8058 uses `codeHash` from the access list, which allows older factories to deploy cost-effective copies. However, EIP-2930 is outdated, so we might consider switching to EIP-7928.
 - Risk on implementation contracts: Allowing code upgrades on already deployed contracts creates a wide-ranging attack vector (all proxies based on it are victims), the case of the Parity wallet (`SELFDESTRUCT`) being typical. However, I'm not saying we can't upgrade, but it needs to be tightly controlled. Note that the authorization indicators of EIP-7702 are fully upgradeable, EIP-7851 removed the ECDSA signing of the account, which is essentially a pure contract. The code for the upgradeable contract will be based on this authorization indicator, and any other code will not be allowed to upgrade.

This is slightly more expensive than supporting `SETCODEFROM` directly in `CREATE`/`CREATE2` initcode, since the factory path needs a small initializer runtime and an extra call. pr_title: Add EIP: SETCODEFROM Code Reuse Instruction
author: CPerezz
body:
This changes EIP-7702’s risk model: today a bad delegate is recoverable by redelegating; with SETCODEFROM reachable from a delegate, the worst case becomes permanent, irreversible loss of key authority. Security Considerations should state this model change explicitly, and the spec should consider mitigations for silent triggering. 

My suggestion:
> Require the indicator→regular-code transition to present a fresh ECDSA-signed commitment by the EOA key over source.codeHash (analogous to 7702’s front-running-initialization mitigation) so a delegate can’t convert the account without an explicit key-signed approval of the exact template.

We can price the opcode higher (due to the ECDSA verification). But it buys us a lot of security for the end-user.

pr_title: Add EIP: SETCODEFROM Code Reuse Instruction
author: colinlyguo
body:
As we already discussed, and also left a comment here, on the ECDSA commitment requirement: I think this is worth discussing, but I'm not fully convinced it should be mandatory. Once an account moves into a 7702-style smart-wallet model, the EOA key may be intentionally de-emphasized, poorly retained, or even generated-and-destroyed for synthetic accounts. In that model, the code path should be able to become the authority.

In my view, users should migrate their normal wallet usage to the smart-account flow before burning or de-emphasizing the private key. Once they do that, the wallet code is the authority they rely on, so requiring another fresh ECDSA approval from the old key may not fit such a security model.

pr_title: Add EIP: SETCODEFROM Code Reuse Instruction
author: jochem-brouwer
body:
```suggestion
Second, it provides an account migration path for disabling ECDSA-based EOA transaction authority. Migration code can store account-specific wallet state, including post-quantum (PQ) wallet state, then adopt regular wallet code. After that update, account control is through the installed wallet code rather than ECDSA transaction origination. This is because the account now has regular deployed code, not an [EIP-7702](./eip-7702.md) delegation indicator, so ECDSA-authenticated transactions remain invalid under [EIP-3607](./eip-3607.md). EIP-7702 authorization processing can no longer redelegate the account because the authority code check only accepts empty code or an existing delegation indicator. The account can still upgrade through upgrade logic in the installed code, for example by calling `SETCODEFROM` again or by using other methods. Protocol-level ECDSA transaction origination remains permanently disabled.
```

EIPs when first mentioned have to be linked.

pr_title: Add EIP: Fixed-Cutoff State Tiering
author: jochem-brouwer
body:
```suggestion
The value is interoperability. If every client writes the Inactive set the same way, the files are interchangeable and can be distributed over ordinary channels such as HTTP and BitTorrent, the same way era files distribute block history. A node can then obtain the cold set from any mirror instead of re-deriving it, which makes dropping it from the hot database practical. Leaving the byte-level encoding to a separate effort keeps this proposal focused on the consensus surcharge.
```

pr_title: Add EIP: Fixed-Cutoff State Tiering
author: CPerezz
body:
Per EIP-8188, several operations bump more than one leaf, but EIP-8296's cost table has one row per leaf type and says __the operation is charged its normal gas plus the corresponding inactive surcharge__ (singular). 

Three concrete cases are undefined:

1. SSTORE to a dormant contract. 8188: an `SSTORE` bumps the slot's last_written_block and the account's (storageRoot recomputed). If both slot and account are Inactive, does the caller pay `INACTIVE_STORAGE_WRITE_SURCHARGE` only, or storage + `INACTIVE_ACCOUNT_WRITE_SURCHARGE`?
2. Value transfer between two dormant accounts. 8188: a balance transfer sets `last_written_block` for both sender and receiver. If both are Inactive, is that one account surcharge or two?
3. Direct collision with __State Creation Is Not Tiered.__ 
Creating a new slot (SSTORE 0→x) in a dormant contract is exempt from the surcharge (it's creation, priced by 8037) — but it cascades an account `storageRoot` mutation, and that account already exists and is Inactive. By the literal rule "tier is evaluated for mutations of state that already exists in the trie," the cascaded account bump would be surcharged. 

So "creation is not tiered" and "Inactive account mutation is surcharged" contradict each other for this very common case.

Extra stuff worth signaling:

4. Another topic is how intrinsic gas should be affected based on this PR.
5. EIP-8037 (same family, explicitly referenced here) splits gas into regular-gas and state-gas, with different block-accounting and a different relationship to EIP-7825's TX_MAX_GAS_LIMIT. EIP-8296 says the surcharge is "consumed like ordinary execution gas," "not refundable," "consumed even on revert" — which reads as regular-gas / single-dimension. But it never reconciles with 8037's two dimensions. Since reviving cold state is I/O work (not state growth), regular-gas is the likely intent — but with 8037 active, this must be explicit, or block-level accounting is undefined.
6. From 8188, legacy (pre-fork, never-rewritten) accounts/slots decode with last_written_block = 0, which is < CUTOFF_BLOCK for any valid cutoff ⇒ Inactive. That's exactly the intent, but 8296 never says it. Also, the inverse edge: state created in [8188_activation, CUTOFF) is Inactive, so its second write pays the surcharge even though it was created recently. Both are consequences worth one explicit sentence each so implementers and users aren't surprised.

pr_title: Update EIP-8037: unfair allocation of EIP-7702 overcharges
author: jochem-brouwer
body:
This makes the calculation of the intrinsic gas cost more expensive, because we now are forced to `ecrecover` all authorizations on the list to account for multiple authorizations for the same address. This is much more expensive than simply doing the authorization count times the possible cost of state creation.

Although I get that this severely overprices authorizations to the same account, I do not see what the use case of doing multiple delegations in the same transaction to the same account: the end result will be a change of the delegation, or no change, and the extra delegations are paid for anyways (in gas cost of at least 12.5k currently).

In order to protect the mempool for authorization-heavy transactions I would stick with the original rule of each transaction having base intrinsic cost which can be refunded. The refund mechanism is something we can change though. 

CC @lightclient who might also have some extra thoughts on this one.

pr_title: Update EIP-8037: unfair allocation of EIP-7702 overcharges
author: jochem-brouwer
body:
Since EIP-8037 will make these authorizations rather expensive (23 * CPSB = 23 * 1530 = 35190 state gas + `ACCOUNT_WRITE` gas depending on EIP-8038) it does make sense to take a look into the gas schedule.

Note that in EIP-7702 the gas is added to the refund counter in case that the account already exists (it is thus not made available as regular gas). Adding it to refund counter is likely a safety mechanism, so we should be careful here.

Actually if I think about this, invalid EIP-7702 authorizations might be used to preload state reservoir which is below the EIP-7825 limit, which is not the intended use case for EIP-7702.

One more comment which changes the gas cost schedule of EIP-7702 which I think we should not do.

Thanks for opening this PR, we should discuss more (I'll open a thread about this on execution-dev on R&D)

pr_title: Add EIP: Post-Quantum Attestation Aggregators
author: jochem-brouwer
body:
```suggestion
Post-Quantum (PQ) Ethereum replaces the beacon chain's BLS signatures with post-quantum, hash-based signatures, which are individually larger than BLS signatures and, unlike BLS, cannot be cheaply combined by adding the signatures themselves. PQ consensus therefore performs attestation aggregation by generating a succinct cryptographic proof that the post-quantum signatures attached to many validator attestations are valid, using a specialized minimal virtual machine. Producing such proofs is far more computationally expensive than the elliptic-curve addition used to aggregate BLS signatures, so the `L*` beacon-chain hard fork separates aggregation from block production and assigns it to an opt-in, higher-specification participant: the *aggregator*. Any node may opt in as an aggregator if it has the hardware to support proving on the slot's critical path. This EIP specifies the aggregator role introduced by the `L*` hard fork; the authoritative definitions of the signature scheme, proof system, wire formats, and consensus rules live in the PQ consensus specification (leanSpec).
```

Define the abbreviation in the text on first use

pr_title: Add EIP: Multi-block Access List Warming
author: jochem-brouwer
body:
"as today", this is not future-proof if we revisit this EIP in 3 forks.


```suggestion
At the start of every transaction in block `B`, the per-tx access list is initialized as: precompiles, `tx.from`, `tx.to`, coinbase per [EIP-3651](./eip-3651.md), [EIP-2930](./eip-2930.md) access list, [EIP-7702](./eip-7702.md) authority list **plus** every item with `WAM[item] > 0`.
```

I think this can be simplified by stating that the access list is initialized as it would be without this EIP, and every item with `WAM[item] > 0` is added as well to the list. This prevents confusion and is also future-proof in case something else in the access list changes. 

Note that currently as stated, if `tx.to` is an EIP-7702 delegated account, this is not added to the access list (while it should be)

pr_title: Add EIP: Multi-block Access List Warming
author: jochem-brouwer
body:
```suggestion
Across blocks, the same items are touched repeatedly. Empirical measurement on 5 731 mainnet blocks shows that **79 % of cold-charged items in a typical block were also touched in the previous 256 blocks** (~51 minutes). Treating those items as already-accessed at the start of the block would eliminate the surcharge they paid, saving **~14 % of total block gas at the median**.
```

pr_title: Add EIP: Frame type for PQ sig and STARK aggregation
author: jochem-brouwer
body:
```suggestion
This EIP extends [EIP-8141](./eip-8141.md) with a new frame mode that enables EVM-level aggregation of cryptographic signatures and STARK (Scalable Transparent ARguments of Knowledge) proofs. The scheme allows transactions to carry lightweight **dependencies** — `(scheme, data_hash, verification_key)` triples — which are aggregated off-chain into a single recursive STARK. Block validity requires this recursive STARK, enabling efficient post-quantum (PQ) and scalable signature aggregation using Lean Ethereum tooling.
```

The title uses the PQ abbreviation (which is fine due to the character limit). It should however be defined somewhere in the document though, such that the reader can figure out what PQ means in this context.

In the current design (KoalaBear field, fixed trace width), this is enforced by the `2**24` trace length limit inherent to KoalaBear, and the trace width is fixed. We want larger proofs (cheaper to generate) to be possible, while still encouraging smaller proofs that put less load on the mempool nodes. This can be achieved by making gas cost proportional to proof size (or a related metric, like query count, and even polynomial degree).

pr_title: Add EIP: Frame type for PQ sig and STARK aggregation
author: jochem-brouwer
body:
```suggestion
Quantum-resistant signatures and zero-knowledge proofs both have a very high calldata requirement and gas cost. Current proposals for hash-based signatures are in the range of ~2-3 kB and ~150,000 to 200,000 gas to verify. Lattice-based signatures have a similar cost. Meanwhile, hash-based zero-knowledge proofs (STARKs) all take over 128 kB, or as much as 512 kB if fast generation is a goal (which it is client-side), which implies a STARK will take many millions of gas to verify. This on its own would mean that privacy protocols will have an impractically high cost, and be completely incompatible with FOCIL ([EIP-7805](./eip-7805.md)) and Frame Transactions ([EIP-8141](./eip-8141.md)).
```

pr_title: Add EIP: Frame type for PQ sig and STARK aggregation
author: b-wagn
body:
I am not sure "up to at least depth 2" is the right framing here. 

The proven relation itself recurses without bounding the depth (the "Verify recursive proofs and collect their deps" loop verifies inner proofs generated by this same relation, so depth is unbounded by construction.) 

The mempool loop described in the EIP also seems to rely on such an unbounded/high-depth recursion. So as far as I understand, the EIP relies on recursion beyond depth 2. 

You do mention unlimited recursion depth, but the "depth 2" phrasing reads as if depth 2 were the default assumption.

pr_title: Add EIP: Frame type for PQ sig and STARK aggregation
author: soispoke
body:
For `LEANSTARK_SCHEME`, is `verification_key` meant to be the full verification key or a 32-byte hash/commitment to it?

If a full leanSTARK verification key does not fit in 32 bytes, the spec should define this field as a `verification_key_hash` or commitment. The full verifier data can then be supplied alongside the proof, or as witness data to the aggregate circuit, and the verifier should check:

hash(canonical_verifier_data) == verification_key 

before running `verify_leanSTARK`.

pr_title: Add EIP: Frame type for PQ sig and STARK aggregation
author: mmjahanara
body:
`block_deps_hash` (and correspondingly the circuit's `deps_hash` public input) should be independent of transaction ordering. As specified, the deps committed by an inner proof are pinned in order by its public input, and the aggregation circuit can only concatenate inner lists; so a builder reusing mode-1 wrappers can only realize dep orderings that are concatenations of the wrappers' committed lists. This can make otherwise-valid transaction sets unincludable:

Suppose each `tx_<address>_<nonce>` declares one dependency `d_<address>_<nonce>`, and the builder receives two wrappers:
```
([tx_a_1, tx_b_2], proof_1)   # commits deps [dep_a_1, dep_b_2]
([tx_a_2, tx_b_1], proof_2)   # commits deps [dep_a_2, dep_b_1]
```
The only reachable dep orderings are `[dep_a_1, dep_b_2, dep_a_2, dep_b_1]` and `[dep_a_2, dep_b_1, dep_a_1, dep_b_2]` and neither is consistent with nonce ordering (tx_a_1 < tx_a_2 and tx_b_1 < tx_b_2). Also re-proving from base witnesses isn't possible for a builder that only received mode-1 wrappers, since the inner witnesses are not retransmitted. So the builder must drop a transaction. The same applies to any order dependent validity condition, it is not just nonce.

One way to fix: define block_deps_hash over the sorted and deduplicated dep list of all transactions in block, and have the circuit sort `filtered_deps`, before asserting `get_deps_hash(filtered_deps) == deps_hash`. The fix addresses block-level duplicate-dependency question/concern raised by @b-wagn as well.

```suggestion
        assert verify_leanSTARK((data_hash,), verification_key, witnesses[i])
```

pr_title: Add EIP: Frame type for PQ sig and STARK aggregation
author: b-wagn
body:
I left some minor comments. Here is my biggest one about security of the recursion:

### Scope / Disclaimer
To be clear up front: I'm not claiming a concrete attack here. This is purely about the usual proof strategy for knowledge soundness — I think the standard argument would not go through as written. Because my proposed fix below seems to be low cost, I would strongly vote for adding it.

### The problem
Knowledge soundness for recursive/PCD proofs is normally argued by recursive extraction: extract the outer witness, observe it contains an inner proof, run the extractor on that, and continue down until we reach a base case (here: a direct signature or a non-recursive STARK). My impression is that if we do this strategy here, with this particular definition of the circuit, this recursive extractor will **not be guaranteed to terminate**: it could be that we are always extracting a single recursive proof (i.e., one for "verify recursive proofs and collect their deps") and continue extracting. There is nothing that guarantees that  our extractor will terminate. Worth emphasizing: this holds even assuming idealized, perfect single-step extractors for the individual STARKs. The gap is not in the per-step extractor (straight-line, believed-sound, whatever), it's in the recursoin. Maybe I am missing something, but I don't see how we guarantee here that we reach the base case. 

### Proposed Fix
The standard way to fix this is to add as a public input a `depth_counter`, which defines the recursive depth. The circuit then must check that this counter is `>= 0` and is decreased when we are in the "verify recursive proofs and collect their deps" part, and that if `depth_counter = 0`, then only the base cases are valid. In this way, if we run one extractor for a public input, we at least decrease the counter by one, meaning that after a finite number of extractions, we must hit a base case and extract a leaf STARK or signature. In the mempool, aggregators need to increase the counters accordingly (something like taking the max of all previous counters + 1). In the block, we would now not only store the top level STARK but also its counter.

My impression is that the overhead from adding this is small, and it buys much more confidence in security.

Note that I don't suggest to limit the recursive depth (this would be against the rationale of the EIP), I just say it is important to keep track of it.

pr_title: Add EIP: Builder Execution Requests
author: jihoonsong
body: This might be interpreted as capping max builder deposits per block solves the signature verification burden. Before EIP-8282, the burden comes from the work of verifying signatures of all pending validators. The capping doesn't solve this issue technically. What solves it is a separation of validator and builder queues, and capping here bounds the builder's signatures verification time.

pr_title: Add EIP: Builder Execution Requests
author: jihoonsong
body:
> A single public key can then be registered as both a validator and a builder; the protocol currently disallows that overlap, and this EIP allows the rule to be removed.

Do you think if it's worth to mention whether this removal has any concern?

pr_title: Add EIP: Builder Execution Requests
author: jihoonsong
body:
```suggestion
- A `BuilderDepositRequest` (type `0x03`) for a `pubkey` **not** yet in the builder set is a first deposit. The consensus layer registers the builder only if both checks pass: its `withdrawal_credentials` begins with the `0x03` `BUILDER_WITHDRAWAL_PREFIX` (`is_builder_withdrawal_credential`), and the proof-of-possession `signature` over the `DepositMessage` `(pubkey, withdrawal_credentials, amount)` under `DOMAIN_BUILDER_DEPOSIT` is valid — the same signature check validator deposits use (gloas `is_valid_deposit_signature`). If both hold, it registers the builder with the record's `withdrawal_credentials` (whose last 20 bytes are the builder's `execution_address`) and credits its `amount`. A record whose `withdrawal_credentials` is not `0x03`-prefixed, or whose signature is invalid, is ignored (consumed, stake forfeited). The prefix check mirrors the credential check `process_deposit_request` applies on the validator path, so a registered builder always carries a `0x03` credential and therefore a well-formed `execution_address`.
```
According to the current spec PR, it uses `DOMAIN_DEPOSIT` for onboarding at fork and `DOMAIN_BUILDER_DEPOSIT` otherwise.

pr_title: Add EIP: Builder Execution Requests
author: jihoonsong
body:
> its `withdrawal_credentials` begins with the `0x03` `BUILDER_WITHDRAWAL_PREFIX` (`is_builder_withdrawal_credential`)

This holds only for onboarding builders at fork.

> The prefix check mirrors the credential check `process_deposit_request` applies on the validator path

This is a bit misleading because `process_deposit_request` doesn't apply any credential check. It stores a credential as-is and the credential is checked during withdrawal.

pr_title: Add EIP: Builder Execution Requests
author: jihoonsong
body: Additionally, I've found withdrawal_credentials[0] is used as a builder version afterward. I think it's good to mention this somewhere. Maybe it can piggyback on this EIP? Not entirely sure though.

pr_title: Add EIP: Builder Execution Requests
author: jihoonsong
body:
> is replaced by `if is_builder_withdrawal_credential(deposit_request.withdrawal_credentials): return`: the deposit is inert — it is **not** appended to `pending_deposits` (so no validator is minted) and its ETH is forfeited in the immutable deposit contract, as with any misdirected deposit.

This is not what the spec PR does. It doesn't change `process_deposit_request` at all, i.e., it doesn't check whether it's a builder deposit. It will create a new validator but it will be impossible to withdraw. My understanding is `process_deposit_request` assumes the request is well-formed. cc @jtraglia

pr_title: Add EIP: Builder Execution Requests
author: jtraglia
body:
A few nits:

> "(gloas `is_valid_deposit_signature`)"

This is not a function introduced in Gloas. I'd just drop the "gloas" word.

> A record whose `withdrawal_credentials` is not `0x03`-prefixed, or whose signature is invalid, is ignored (consumed, stake forfeited).

Not true. Any prefix (version) is valid. They could use 0x00 - 0xFF.

> The prefix check mirrors the credential check `process_deposit_request` applies on the validator path, so a registered builder always carries a `0x03` credential and therefore a well-formed `execution_address`.

I would just delete this.

pr_title: Add EIP: Builder Execution Requests
author: jtraglia

pr_title: Add EIP: Builder Execution Requests
author: jtraglia
body: Hmm not sure I agree. I think it is more like a voluntary exit. The only reason we'd want to check that the version is a specific value would be to incentivize builders use supported versions; ie don't make a builder with version=0xFF. But I don't think this is a strong enough reason to do this, as I expect some builders to accidentally use the 0x03 withdrawal credential with the new contract.

author: Helkomine
body:
> No log is emitted for self-transfers as per https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-7708

So, should we update EIP-7708 to remove the case where log is not emitted for self-transfer? This would reduce the number of test branches and accurately reflect the behavior of ERC-20.

pr_title: Update EIP-2780: precompile target and account-warming charge changes
author: benaadams
body:
> > No log is emitted for self-transfers as per https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-7708
>  So, should we update EIP-7708 to remove the case where log is not emitted for self-transfer? This would reduce the number of test branches and accurately reflect the behavior of ERC-20.

Don't see why, EIP-7708 is live on devnets and has active tests. Its motivation is to surface balance changes and self-transfer isn't a balance transfer.

ERC20 have custom transfer implementations (could be fee-on-transfer) so a self-transfer isn't necessarily idempotent

pr_title: Update EIP-2780: precompile target and account-warming charge changes
author: Helkomine
body:
> 
> Don't see why, EIP-7708 is live on devnets and has active tests. Its motivation is to surface balance changes and self-transfer isn't a balance transfer.
> 
> ERC20 have custom transfer implementations (could be fee-on-transfer) so a self-transfer isn't necessarily idempotent

I believe the protocol is overcomplicating things with minor interface details while simultaneously cutting meaningful incentives for the same reason. For example, retaining self-transfer verification branches while reducing the transaction access list discount. We're wasting effort on something the interface can handle instead of prioritizing transaction performance.

pr_title: Update EIP-2780: precompile target and account-warming charge changes
author: gurukamath
body:
> > To clarify self-transfer is already special cased in Eip-7708 to not emit a log (as no ETH moves); so why do we charge for LOG + transfer if neither happens?
> 
> That makes sense and will change the PR. The intention was to remove the gas discount. I don't have a strong stance, but I would feel better if it is priced the same.

Charging the same gas for self and other transfers make sense to me from a design simplicity perspective. Yes, that means we end up charging an extra emit log costs for self transfers where a log never gets emitted. But I think self-transfers are too niche to carve out an exception for. Perhaps we should just explicitly document this trade-off in the EIP text to make it clear that this is a deliberate call that has been made.

pr_title: Update EIP-2780: precompile target and account-warming charge changes
author: abc-123-c
body:
> > 
> > That makes sense and will change the PR. The intention was to remove the gas discount. I don't have a strong stance, but I would feel better if it is priced the same.
> 
> Charging the same gas for self and other transfers make sense to me from a design simplicity perspective. Yes, that means we end up charging an extra emit log costs for self transfers where a log never gets emitted. But I think self-transfers are too niche to carve out an exception for. Perhaps we should just explicitly document this trade-off in the EIP text to make it clear that this is a deliberate call that has been made.

I agree there shouldn't be any discount for self-transfer, but could we still maintain emitting for it? We would make the implementation even simpler if we eliminated that exception.

pr_title: Update EIP-2780: precompile target and account-warming charge changes
author: benaadams
body:
> > Don't see why, EIP-7708 is live on devnets and has active tests. Its motivation is to surface balance changes and self-transfer isn't a balance transfer.
> > ERC20 have custom transfer implementations (could be fee-on-transfer) so a self-transfer isn't necessarily idempotent
> 
> while reducing the transaction access list discount. 

EIP-7981 repricing makes access lists not sensible to use other than in their original justification (which was unbricking some contracts) https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-7981

They are essentially deprecated; also they add no value to `To` since its already specified ahead of time so including it in a access list is just duplication

pr_title: Update EIP-2780: precompile target and account-warming charge changes
author: Helkomine
body:
> 
> EIP-7981 repricing makes access lists not sensible to use other than in their original justification (which was unbricking some contracts) https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-7981
> 
> They are essentially deprecated; also they add no value to `To` since its already specified ahead of time so including it in a access list is just duplication

Yes, that example is not reasonable ; it would be more appropriate to compare using precompiled contracts.
 
However, I see one aspect of this EIP that isn't optimized for ETH to compete with ERC-20: the `STATE_UPDATE` fee when transferring ETH. It would be better to separate it into cold and warm price tiers, similar to the storage slots of ERC-20. We already have EIP-2200 to address reentrancy, so I think we should relax this part further.

pr_title: Update EIP-8037: improve EIP-7702 authorization gas accounting in EIP-8037
author: misilva73
body:
Building on the rule‑4 issue already raised above — rather than fixing how `billed` gets populated, I think the whole set can be dropped. `billed` is reconstructing something that's already in current state: once an earlier authorization delegates `A`, its `codeHash` is non-empty, so "was this authority delegated earlier in the tx?" is just a `codeHash` check. The only thing current state can't distinguish is *pre-tx* vs *in-tx* delegation, which matters solely for the cancel case and is a single read of the pre-tx snapshot.

That collapses the 5 rules to 3. It's equivalent to the intended behavior — the rule‑3 condition `pre_delegated OR billed OR ZERO` is exactly `cur_delegated OR pre_delegated OR ZERO` once `billed = cur_delegated AND NOT pre_delegated` — but reading `codeHash` directly can't have the rule‑4 failure mode, and it fixes `0→a→0` for funded EOAs (which rule 5 misses today because those authorities never enter `billed`).

Concrete suggestion (also drops the `billed` set, fixes the "state state" typo, and tidies rule 1's grammar):

```suggestion
The adjustments enforce a single invariant: the `STATE_BYTES_PER_NEW_ACCOUNT × CPSB` account-leaf portion is charged at most once per authority and only when the account did not exist before the transaction, and the `STATE_BYTES_PER_AUTH_BASE × CPSB` delegation-indicator portion is charged at most once per authority and only when the authority ends the transaction delegated having started it undelegated.

Processing reads the account state at two points:

- **pre-transaction state**: the account state before transaction execution.
- **current state**: the account state while processing authorizations, updated after each authorization. Because an in-transaction delegation leaves a delegation indicator in the authority's `code` field, the current state already records whether an earlier authorization in this transaction delegated the same authority.

For each authorization, let `cur_delegated` be `true` when the authority has a non-empty delegation indicator in the **current state** (`codeHash != emptyHash`), and `pre_delegated` be `true` when it had one in the **pre-transaction state**. Authorization processing follows 3 gas accounting rules:

**1. Invalid authorizations.** Invalid authorizations are skipped without per-auth processing. Their entire intrinsic state-gas portion, `(STATE_BYTES_PER_NEW_ACCOUNT + STATE_BYTES_PER_AUTH_BASE) × CPSB`, is refilled to `state_gas_reservoir` and `ACCOUNT_WRITE` is refunded to the refund counter.

**2. Account-leaf refill.** If the authority's account leaf already exists in the **current state** (non-zero nonce, non-zero balance, or non-empty code), refill `STATE_BYTES_PER_NEW_ACCOUNT × CPSB` to `state_gas_reservoir` and refund `ACCOUNT_WRITE` to the refund counter.

**3. Delegation-indicator refill.**

- If `authorization.address` is not `ZERO` (setting a delegation), refill `STATE_BYTES_PER_AUTH_BASE × CPSB` to `state_gas_reservoir` when `cur_delegated` or `pre_delegated` is `true`. In that case the 23-byte indicator slot is already occupied, so this authorization overwrites it without writing new bytes. Otherwise this authorization performs the net-new creation and its intrinsic charge stands.
- If `authorization.address` is `ZERO` (clearing the delegation), refill `STATE_BYTES_PER_AUTH_BASE × CPSB` to `state_gas_reservoir`, since the clear writes no indicator. Additionally, when `cur_delegated` is `true` and `pre_delegated` is `false`, refill another `STATE_BYTES_PER_AUTH_BASE × CPSB`: the delegation being cleared was created by an earlier authorization in this same transaction, so the chain writes zero net delegation bytes and the earlier creation charge is no longer justified. This covers patterns such as `0->a->0`, where the creation by an earlier authorization is undone by a later clearing one in the same list.
```

Reads as a description of *what* changed but doesn't explain *why* the envelope no longer commits to a post-state root. A reader comparing old vs. new will notice `state_root` (and `slot`) are gone from `ExecutionPayloadEnvelope` and wonder what motivated it.

The design shift: previously the envelope mutated state, so it had to commit to the post-state-transition root. Now that state application moves into the next block's `process_parent_execution_payload`, envelope verification is stateless relative to the parent — so the post-state commitment is no longer needed.

Suggest folding one sentence to that effect into this paragraph, otherwise the dropped fields look unmotivated.

pr_title: Update EIP-8141: Extend with Guarantors, Flexible Nonces, and Signer Binding
author: AnkushinDaniil
body:
Nice consolidation - folding guarantors, keyed nonces, and signer binding under one `AUTH_MANAGER` with a single `signer` field is a clean idea, and unifying the nonce channel with the registered pubkey is neat when you want both together.

One tradeoff worth surfacing on the keyed-nonce part vs EIP-8250: here a non-zero `signer` is only valid if a signer entry already exists at `(sender, signer)`, so a parallel nonce channel needs a registered signer first. EIP-8250's `(nonce_keys, nonce_seq)` keys are arbitrary and need no registration, which keeps the nonce namespace decoupled from signer identity - handy for parallel nonces on a single-key wallet, or ephemeral one-time nonce keys. I think that decoupling is worth keeping - wdyt about the two shapes?

Also, since guarantors (#11555) and keyed nonces (8250) are already their own threads, pulling the pieces apart might land easier than one big change, and it looks like this needs a rebase against current master (CI is red). Happy to help reconcile the keyed-nonce part with 8250 if useful.

author: amiecorso
body: one thing I'm noticing missing from the spec is any limitation on the scope of a policy-managed key (i.e. not restricted only to `SENDER` scope). Is the idea here that this shouldn't be defined at the protocol level but rather any given key that's authorized can decide for itself whether it needs to limit payer scope to avoid gas griefing?

author: amiecorso
body: I would maybe upgrade the "SHOULD" language here to a "MUST" and it might be worth noting here that policies and managers should also be non-upgradeable otherwise it's equivalent to root access.

pr_title: Update EIP-8130: Add owner call policies
author: amiecorso
body: I like this per-policy manager optionality v.s. having a protocol-defined canonical manager. unlocks the manager=account scenario as you described and is just overall more flexible

pr_title: Update EIP-8130: Add owner call policies
author: amiecorso
body: definitely support native expiry... both in the context of policies and just in general for authorized keys

pr_title: Update EIP-8130: Add owner call policies
author: chunter-cb
body:
Good catch — addressed in 13ca60eb. The gate only covers SENDER-context calls, so this is no longer left implicit: a policy-bearing owner (`policyType != 0x00`) is now rejected at authorization if its scope is unrestricted (`0x00`) or includes CONFIG (`0x08`) — a CONFIG-scoped key could authorize new, unrestricted owners and escape its own policy (i.e. root).

PAYER and SIGNATURE remain wallet choices but are now explicitly documented as *not* policy-constrained (PAYER allows gas griefing up to the tx limits; SIGNATURE allows ERC-1271 signatures the policy never sees), with guidance to grant a restricted key only the scopes it needs — typically SENDER alone. Changes: a **Scope** paragraph in Owner Policies, the reject rule in create/`authorizeOwner`, and a sentence in the Owner Scope and Policy security item.

pr_title: Update EIP-8130: Add owner call policies
author: chunter-cb
body:
Added the non-upgradeable caveat in 13ca60eb: an upgradeable manager lets whoever controls the upgrade rewrite enforcement, which is equivalent to root access over everything the manager can do for the account.

On SHOULD vs MUST: I kept SHOULD for the *audited* / *non-upgradeable* guidance, since those are off-chain properties the protocol cannot verify and RFC-2119 MUST reads poorly for unenforceable advice. The one place it is a hard **MUST** is the new scope restriction (above), which the protocol actually enforces at authorization. Happy to tighten the wording if you feel strongly.

pr_title: Update EIP-2780: Rework as resource-based intrinsic transaction gas
author: misilva73
body: No double-charge here, because the two accesses hit different accounts. The `COLD_ACCOUNT_ACCESS` in `REGULAR_PER_AUTH_BASE_COST` pays for reading the nonce and code of the authority (the EOA being delegated, i.e. the account at the tx.to address). The additional `COLD_ACCOUNT_ACCESS` in this phase pays for resolving the delegation — following the 0xef0100‖address pointer to load the delegate target's code, a different account. So even when the authorization materializes the delegation in the same transaction, it only prepays the authority touch, not the target-code read.

1 - I agree should clean up the language here. The implicit verifier must be used for the default path (it is coded that way in the contract) https://github.com/ethereum/EIPs/pull/11654
2 - This is fair and addressed in https://github.com/ethereum/EIPs/pull/11654

pr_title: Update EIP-8130: Add create entry existing-account and code-size guards
author: chunter-cb
body:
Agree on enforcing the EIP-170 max code size.

For the existing-account guard, I think the clean rule is simply to match CREATE2 freshness semantics: the create entry should fail under the same destination-account conditions that CREATE2 would fail under. That means checking code/nonzero nonce rather than inventing separate EIP-8130-specific freshness rules.

I’m less convinced by the owner_config emptiness check. If code already exists, create fails. If code does not exist, then any existing owner config is effectively EOA-style state, and deriving a create entry to that same EOA address is infeasible under normal address-preimage assumptions. We could consider checking that the account’s change sequences are both zero as a simple lifecycle guard, but I don’t think enumerating or requiring no owner_config entries is the right rule.

pr_title: Add EIP: Blob Streaming
author: jochem-brouwer
body:
```suggestion
Ethereum's current blob data availability design, introduced in [EIP-4844](./eip-4844.md) and extended with PeerDAS ([EIP-7594](./eip-7594.md)), hinges on blob data propagation on the critical path. While pre-propagation of blob data through the EL blobpool is possible, it comes with no upper bounds on the load being handled and as such can lead to inconsistent local node views - which in turn translates to vulnerability to DoS attacks especially if pre-propagation is coupled with data-availability sampling (DAS). 
```

(Denial-of-Service usually abbreviated as DoS)

For readability, suggestion to link to EIP-7805 earlier.
```suggestion
This EIP does not include mechanisms for mandatory inclusion of AOT blob transactions. While ticket transactions can be included in [FOCIL ILs (EIP-7805)](./eip-7805.md), a builder can still censor by observing that AOT data is available yet choosing not to include the corresponding transaction. Addressing this requires forced inclusion lists (e.g., EIP-7805) and PTC availability voting, which are left to future work to avoid coupling this proposal to those designs.
```

author: nerolation
body:
With EIP-7928 and snap/2, clients will keep 3533 epochs (=WSP) of BALs around and would need to re-sync if there was a reorg deeper than that period.
Similar to snap/1, if a reorg exceeds the client’s retained/recoverable state horizon, the client must re-sync state instead of processing the reorg incrementally using state diffs. In snap/2 that horizon is the WSP. In geth f.e. snap sync today it is effectively bounded by the locally recoverable snap/pivot state, after which geth falls back to snap sync again.
So, you're right that the max reorg could be ~8,678 (38d) with 75% of validators offline, it's here also a trade off between how many BALs/state diffs we want to keep around before we snap sync again. Note, snap sync starts at HEAD-64 and not the finalized block.
Today, some EL clients only support reorgs of depth 128, which is the main rational behind this change - ensuring it's more than just 128 before triggering re-sync.
I will put this on today's ACD agenda for discussion. It feels like we could also increase the BAL retention period to 38 days and then be able to use the finalized block as the first pivot in snap/2.

> With EIP-7928 and snap/2, clients will keep 3533 epochs (=WSP)

Sounds like the same argument could be made for 7928 then ;) ie semantically, we will never reorg deeper than finality so this seems like a worthy target - consensus clients are expected to handle reorgs exactly that deep but this of course relies on execution clients following suit.

>  Today, some EL clients only support reorgs of depth 128,

I see this as a quality-of-implementation issue more than anything, ie we can state an expectation in the spec and then clients do what they will with it - not supporting deep reorgs means that the user manually must get involved in ethereum recovery - but it's also important to align EL and CL on this point since otherwise we'll be wasting resources on at least one of the sides of the coin - there's scant reason to have CL's support deep reorgs as they do without the underlying EL support present.

pr_title: Add EIP: Execution-Layer Reorg State Retention Window
author: nerolation
body:
Agree but one difference there is that "handling reorgs" on the EL can be done in two ways, rolling back or resyncing.
Snap sync uses HEAD-64 as the first pivot block and doesn't anchor on a finalized checkpoint, thus clients can handle such reorgs. The question is more "how" (resync vs rolling back), and here we argue that rolling back should be possible until WSP, whereas everything beyond that requires resyncing state.
For snap/1 and /2, nodes must resync if they don't have enough state diffs around to rewind state.
BALs won't help there as they're one-directional (only have the post-state and not the pre-state) and can only  be used in the healing phase.

As of https://github.com/ethereum/EIPs/blob/3f561dfb7e27299479ff8aac3359819547965b72/EIPS/eip-1.md we have:

`An Informational EIP describes an Ethereum design issue, or provides general guidelines or information to the Ethereum community, but does not propose a new feature. Informational EIPs do not necessarily represent Ethereum community consensus or a recommendation, so users and implementers are free to ignore Informational EIPs or follow their advice.`

I believe this EIP is a hard requirement ("MUST" by RFC 2119) and this can thus not be ignored, and therefore this cannot be Informational.

pr_title: Add EIP: Execution-Layer Reorg State Retention Window
author: jochem-brouwer
body:
```suggestion
For every canonical block `B` with `head.number - B.number <= REORG_RETENTION_WINDOW`, EL clients MUST be able to reconstruct `B`'s post-state using only locally-stored data, without requesting any data over the network. The representation (full snapshots, reverse state diffs, or any equivalent) and its location (memory or disk) are unspecified. State older than the window MAY be discarded.
```

(nit: this assumes head.number >= B.number, since we are talking about reorgs I think this is implicit, and we are talking about the canonical chain also)

Note that this fixes the possible off-by-one also. If the `REORG_RETENTION_WINDOW` is 1, we actually have access to 2 post-states: namely, the head block and the head block minus 1.

body:
> What is the verifier "cost"? Is this runtime?
Correct, it is runtime. 

The "witnessed computation" is payload execution. I agree that having the term "witnessed computation" adds a layer of indirection and confusion, so maybe we can say something like "in the size `n` of the payload execution trace" or possibly "in the number of computation cycles `n` of payload execution". Happy for you to make a proposal on this.

`n` attempts to capture the analogous concept of CPU cycle count in the proof system domain. The concrete value `n` is a combination of guest program efficiency (consider this analogous to reth vs geth, for example) and zkVM efficiency (consider this analogous to ARM vs x86). 

> I am also confused, because this seems to imply this O(log²n) is "the scale" here. I would assume this depends on the proof system (?).

Correct, but we are currently only interested in STARK-based proof systems which follow this scale. If we want to be more generic, we can consider changing this scale to polylog(n) rather than log^2(n).

What if we make this rule more aggressive: like, a batch is ignored if less than a half of its attesting indices are unseen. In this case `SingleAttestation` and any batch containing that attestation won’t suppress each other, at the same time the attack complexity reduces to `O(log(k))`.

Higher information density per committee => fewer messages => fewer bytes on the wire per committee => merge committees while keeping traffic constant => fewer slots per epoch => shorter epochs. What if we keep it as as placeholder for now, so it remains easy to frame the benefits in a single spec, then spin it off later?

author: raulk
body:
Right, good flag. If V both submits a SingleAttestation and participates in a batch, the current proposal races. If the SingleAttestation arrives first, it can block the batch from being accepted, **unless the client deconflicts** and evicts it in favour of the stronger batch.

This race could occur if V decides to attest independently in addition to participating in a batch. This could happen as an operational fallback, or as malicious behaviour.

Generally speaking, the current version assumes high trust between the VC and the beacon node. That assumption may not hold in DVT, LST, and other staking designs. It would be good to loop in various teams and pressure-test against their specific assumptions.

I think you meant to break this sentence?

> Failure to do so before payment has been approved will result in the whole transaction being invalid after payment has been approved, the frame is treated as a paid failure.

pr_title: Update EIP-8141: allow payer to approve before sender
author: derekchiang
body:
Also, if a VERIFY frame after payment has been approved does NOT call `APPROVE` at all, is the transaction valid or not?  The rest of the spec would suggest that VERIFY frames MUST call approve, but the way this is written makes it sound like it's OK to not call `APPROVE` as long as payment has been approved.

My suggestion would be:

- Before payment is approved, VERIFY frames MUST **successfully** call `APPROVE` for the transaction to be valid
- After payment is approved, VERIFY frames MUST call `APPROVE` for the transaction to be valid, but `APPROVE` may fail without invalidating the transaction.

Not sure if that's clear or confusing.

pr_title: Update EIP-8141: allow payer to approve before sender
author: derekchiang
body:
Shouldn't we update the canonical paymaster code so it can be safely used in a payer-first txn?  Otherwise the usefulness of this update is severely limited, since the public mempool only allows 1 pending txn per non-canonical paymaster.

I implemented a replay protection mechanism here: https://github.com/ethereum/EIPs/pull/11555.  Though since we don't have an explicit approval scope for guarantors in this PR, the guarantor code path would need to have the additional logic of checking its frame position.

body: It's not helpful to specify "replay-protection writes" right?  Since it's not clear how the client would enforce that.  I think we just need to make the canonical paymaster handle replay, and canonical paymaster can do state writes because of the canonical paymaster exception.

pr_title: Update EIP-8037: fixed CPSB + frame accounting
author: abc-123-c
body:
> This is not possible. A self-destructed account can still be called during execution and, in that scenario, the gas accounting will be a mess. We need to give the refund at the point where the account is destroyed, which is at the end of transaction.

Can you provide more details about the implementation issues? According to eip6780, an account still has execution logic after a selfdestruct operation. However, we cannot redeploy that address due to eip684. Therefore, we are left with only one option: revert. We can apply similar semantics to sstore. I know this isn't ideal, but it's necessary to support temporary contracts because we don't have dedicated opcodes for them, and also because late refunds wouldn't be possible on Monad because the amount of gas consumed is based on the gas limit, not the amount of gas used. We also expect that the gas supply should be used as efficiently as possible, as it is locked in until the end of the transaction.

body:
I disagree. Unless there's a dedicated opcode snippet, the `CREATE`/`SELFDESTRUCT` pattern is still useful for creating ephemeral contracts. For example, we could save `120 x cpsb` by removing a `CREATE3` proxy : https://etherscan.io/address/0xfe752dc15cc4cbaefe5308d6de740b10be48cb7a#code

Also, on Monad, gas consumption is gas limit, so refunding at the end of the transaction doesn't seem very efficient.

pr_title: Update EIP-8037: Proposal for Revising 8037
author: jochem-brouwer
body:
I left some comments.

The main problem I currently see with this is that (if I understand the gas mechanism here correctly, which I am not sure about: I see the original state before the transaction and the state after the transaction (without doing state check yet) and for all created state we charge the associated gas, and revert tx if it cannot be paid for).

The problem I have with this is that there are situations where it is clear that there is insufficient gas to pay for the creation, but only at the very end of the transaction this is checked: the user has executed a lot of compute opcodes and still has to pay for those. There is also a problem where if you call an unknown contract this could now spam state creation such that either the user has to pay a massive fee (if they provided a very high gas limit) or the tx reverts, causing the user to waste gas on computation.

Also note that this approach changes EIP-7702: in that EIP, the delegations are not rolled back in case the entire transaction reverts. This now seems to change, if there is insufficient gas then also do not create the accounts (or delegation code of 23 bytes)

body:
I think this is missing the parent reference that makes this a binding accumulator across both chains. I believe it should be something like seen below with the parent_chain_binding_hash as input:
```
chain_binding_hash = SHA256(
      parent_chain_binding_hash,
      beacon_parent_root,
      prev_randao,
      timestamp,
      slot_number,
      expected_withdrawals_hash,
      execution_requests_hash,
      blob_versioned_hashes_hash,
  )
``` 

I removed the `gas_limit` because I couldn't find any constraints on it in the CL specs, and as such, it may not be needed.

pr_title: Update EIP-8141: Tighten spec
author: Copilot
body:
`FRAMEINFO` param `0x07` says it returns `frame.flags & 0x04` and also that it "returns 0/1". The expression `frame.flags & 0x04` returns `0` or `4`, not `0` or `1`. Either define the return value as `0/4`, or change the definition to a boolean/bit value (e.g., `(frame.flags >> 2) & 1`).
```suggestion
| `param` | `frameIndex` | Return value                                              |
|---------|--------------|-----------------------------------------------------------|
| 0x00    | frameIndex   | `target`                                                  |
| 0x01    | frameIndex   | `gas_limit`                                               |
| 0x02    | frameIndex   | `mode`                                                    |
| 0x03    | frameIndex   | `flags`                                                   |
| 0x04    | frameIndex   | `len(data)`                                               |
| 0x05    | frameIndex   | `status` (exceptional halt if current/future)             |
| 0x06    | frameIndex   | `allowed_scope` (`frame.flags & APPROVE_SCOPE_MASK`)      |
| 0x07    | frameIndex   | `atomic_batch` (`(frame.flags >> 2) & 0x01`, returns 0/1) |
```

pr_title: Update EIP-8141: Tighten spec
author: Copilot
body:
The doc comment says the contract calls `APPROVE(0x1)` to approve payment, but the `APPROVE` opcode (per the spec in this PR) consumes `offset`, `length`, and `scope` from the stack. Consider clarifying that this implementation calls `APPROVE` with `scope=0x1` and `offset/length=0` to avoid suggesting a single-argument ABI-style call.
```suggestion
///      On success, the contract calls APPROVE with scope=0x1 and offset/length=0 to approve payment.
```

pr_title: Add EIP: Counterfactual Transaction
author: Copilot
body:
`FEE_DENOMINATIONS` are specified as decimal "ETH" values (e.g., `0.001 ETH`). Since these values are consensus-critical and compared to `msg.value` / `gas_limit * max_fee_per_gas`, it would be clearer and less error-prone to specify them as exact integer wei amounts (and/or explicitly define the conversion).
```suggestion
| `FEE_DENOMINATIONS` | `1000000000000000 wei` (`0.001 ETH`), `10000000000000000 wei` (`0.01 ETH`), `100000000000000000 wei` (`0.1 ETH`), `1000000000000000000 wei` (`1 ETH`), `5000000000000000000 wei` (`5 ETH`) |
```

pr_title: Add EIP: Contract Payer Transaction
author: Copilot
body:
The spec requires the gas-funding and refund-return transfers to “emit an EIP-7708 Transfer log”, but it doesn’t define the exact consensus-visible log details for these protocol-level transfers (emitting address, topics/data encoding, and ordering relative to other logs in the receipt). Please specify these explicitly so clients can implement deterministic receipt/log generation (especially for the post-execution refund-return log).
```suggestion
Every balance transfer in the [Transaction Execution](#transaction-execution) steps is a real state change. The two new transfers introduced by this EIP - the gas funding (step 2, `tx.to` -> `sender`) and the refund return (step 7, `sender` -> `tx.to`) - MUST each emit exactly one [EIP-7708](./eip-7708.md) `Transfer` log.

For both of these transfers, the consensus-visible log MUST use the same emitting `address`, topic layout, indexed fields, and data encoding that [EIP-7708](./eip-7708.md) specifies for any ETH transfer log. In particular, clients MUST NOT use `sender` or `tx.to` as a special-case log-emitting address for these protocol-level transfers; the log `address` is whatever [EIP-7708](./eip-7708.md) defines for ETH transfer logs, and the encoded transfer endpoints and amount are `(from=tx.to, to=sender, value=gas_limit * max_fee_per_gas)` for step 2 and `(from=sender, to=tx.to, value=unused_gas * effective_gas_price)` for step 7.

These two logs are included in the transaction receipt in execution order. The gas-funding log for step 2 is emitted before any logs produced by executing the transaction call. The refund-return log for step 7 is emitted after all logs produced during execution, because it is generated only after final gas accounting determines the refund amount. This ordering is consensus-critical.

Because the sender actually holds and pays the gas, receipts, `effectiveGasPrice`, and all other gas-related logs work identically to [EIP-1559](./eip-1559.md) transactions, except for the addition of the two explicitly-defined [EIP-7708](./eip-7708.md) logs above. No synthetic logs are introduced beyond those required to represent these real transfers.
```

```suggestion
Lean Staking can be post-quantum secure provided the underlying proving system is as well. We provide an implementation using LeanVM, an ongoing Ethereum Foundation project, which is envisioned as a formally verified and post-quantum ready proving system. pr_title: Update EIP-8189: Use RLP empty str placeholder, add bytes parameter to GetBlockAccessLists
```
author: rjl493456442
body:
The rationale for choosing the rlp.EmptyString for representing the absent BAL is:

- rlp.EmptyList represents an empty BAL, which is semantically distinct.
- The network packet returns a list of BALs, where each element is encoded as rlp.RawBytes. Since this is a list (not a union), all elements must share the same type, making rlp.EmptyString the only valid optional value.
- []byte{} is not a valid RLP element.

pr_title: Update EIP-2780: Add transfer log cost, remove PAY
author: Copilot
body: `TRANSFER_LOG_COST` is introduced here, but the later intrinsic-gas section doesn’t appear to actually charge it for top-level `tx.value > 0` transfers (the normative `CalculateIntrinsicGas` pseudocode only adds `GAS_NEW_ACCOUNT`), and the test vectors still state that `value > 0` to a precompile is intrinsic `4,500`. Please update the intrinsic-gas rules/pseudocode and test vectors to either (a) add `TRANSFER_LOG_COST` for any nonzero-value transfer to a different account (including precompiles, per EIP-7708), or (b) explicitly specify and justify any exemptions.

pr_title: Update EIP-2780: Add transfer log cost, remove PAY
author: Copilot
body: `CALL_VALUE_COST` is defined here as always including `TRANSFER_LOG_COST`, but EIP-7708 only emits the transfer log when the value transfer is to a *different* account. For value-carrying self-calls (`caller == to`), no log should be emitted, so charging `TRANSFER_LOG_COST` would be inconsistent with both EIP-7708 and the later self-transfer exception for top-level txs. Consider making the `TRANSFER_LOG_COST` component conditional on `caller != to` (and documenting the behavior explicitly).

pr_title: Update EIP-2780: Add transfer log cost, remove PAY
author: Copilot
body:
This paragraph says `TRANSFER_LOG_COST` is applied to top-level value transfers and value-moving `CALL`s, but EIP-7708 also emits a transfer log for nonzero-value `SELFDESTRUCT` to a different account. If this EIP intends to charge explicitly for the EIP-7708 transfer log, please also specify how/where `TRANSFER_LOG_COST` is charged for `SELFDESTRUCT`-based value transfers (or explicitly state why they’re exempt).
```suggestion
- **[EIP-7708](./eip-7708.md) (ETH transfers emit a log).** EIP-7708 emits a LOG3 transfer event for every nonzero-value ETH transfer. Under the legacy `21,000` base this cost was absorbed; with a reduced base it must be charged explicitly. This EIP introduces `TRANSFER_LOG_COST = 1,756` (LOG3 equivalent: `375 + 3×375 + 32×8`) applied to top-level value transfers, value-moving `CALL`s, and nonzero-value `SELFDESTRUCT` when it transfers value to a different account; for `SELFDESTRUCT`, the charge is applied at the point that transfer is processed.
```

pr_title: Update EIP-8141: add signatures list to outer tx
author: derekchiang
body: I feel that one practical difficulty with smart contracts leveraging these outer signatures is that it's not clear what index a smart contract should use.  The contract can't simply hardcode an index because the transaction may have any number of signatures and may order the signatures arbitrarily.  This weakness can be seen in [the updated default code](https://github.com/ethereum/EIPs/pull/11481/changes#diff-fa7f710dbdc2909318c31c817ef313f90df424946ea1a162d13406806b7f1d92R456-R459), where it has to loop through the signature list to find the one it needs.

pr_title: Update EIP-8141: add signatures list to outer tx
author: 0xrcinus
body:
An idea:

If the `tx.sender` has a signature in `signatures` which is signing the `sig_hash`, no further `VERIFY` frame is required to approve the sender. If there isn't a paymaster `VERIFY` frame, this also sets the `sender` as the `payer`.

If another account has a signature in `signatures` which is signing the `sig_hash`, they have agreed to pay for the transaction.

So then the frames themselves can just be pure execution.

pr_title: Update EIP-8141: add signatures list to outer tx
author: morph-dev
body:
> An idea:
> 
> If the `tx.sender` has a signature in `signatures` which is signing the `sig_hash`, no further `VERIFY` frame is required to approve the sender. If there isn't a paymaster `VERIFY` frame, this also sets the `sender` as the `payer`.
> 
> If another account has a signature in `signatures` which is signing the `sig_hash`, they have agreed to pay for the transaction.
> 
> So then the frames themselves can just be pure execution.

This isn't good idea. Some accounts could have custom validation logic that doesn't rely only on `sig_hash` (or at all).

For example, we could have smart wallet that uses key rotation. If private key associated with "sender" is revealed/leaked after key was rotated, attacker would simply create tx that is signed with "sender" but it bypass smart wallet's validation logic.

pr_title: Update EIP-8141: add signatures list to outer tx
author: 0xrcinus
body:
> This isn't good idea. Some accounts could have custom validation logic that doesn't rely only on sig_hash (or at all)

Sure, I should have clarified that this would only apply for default EOAs (conventional smart wallets don't have signing keys, and this should also exclude 7702-delegated EOAs... there is not currently a way to rotate an EOA key, but if that is introduced as in EIP-8164 that should also be taken into account, though to be clear I think that would also happen automatically as the original key would no longer be valid).

pr_title: Update EIP-8037: clarify state gas behavior on frame failure (child vs top-level)
author: misilva73
body:
The general principle we tried to follow when setting the logic to `state_gas` refills on failure cases was "state gas pays for long-term state growth which does not occur on failure." This principle is applied consistently for child frames (state gas restored to parent on revert/halt). However, the current spec (and this proposal of updating the EIP) does not apply this at the top level, which is not an obvious choice.

Arguments for restoring state gas on topmost revert/halt:

- Consistency with child frame behavior. The asymmetry is hard to justify — why does the same revert logic differ based on call depth? At depth 1, state gas is fully reclaimed by the parent. At depth 0, it's lost. This creates a surprising edge case.
- `block_state_gas_used` should reflect reality. If it's meant to track how much state the block actually grew, counting reverted state operations inflates it. A block that reverted all its state-touching transactions would hit the state gas limit despite growing zero state.

Arguments against restoring state gas on topmost revert/halt:

- Pre-EIP-8037 precedent. `GAS_NEW_ACCOUNT` (25,000 gas) is consumed on revert today. The EIP's "Revert behavior" section explicitly preserves this behavior. 

My first intuition is that restoring the state gas in this case would make more sense. am I missing som edge case where this behavior would not make sense in the topmost frame? Why was `GAS_NEW_ACCOUNT` originally spent in cases where no account was created?

pr_title: Add EIP: Block-scoped transient storage opcodes
author: jochem-brouwer
body:
```suggestion
[EIP-1153](./eip-1153.md) introduced transaction-scoped transient storage, enabling cheap inter-frame communication within a single transaction. However, there is no equivalent mechanism for cheap state that persists across transactions within the same block. Currently, contracts that need to maintain block-level state — such as cumulative values, per-block rate limits, or block-local registries — must use persistent storage (`SSTORE (0x55)`/`SLOAD (0x54)`), paying the full cost of disk serialization for data that is only meaningful for the duration of a single block.
```

(see https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-1#special-requirements-for-core-eips)


Ah, never mind, I thought it was intended to store a `value` at another `address` (another account (EOA or contract). This is not the case. The "address" is confusing here, I suggest `slot` as you use later in the sentence also.


```suggestion
`BLOAD` pops one 32-byte word `slot` from the top of the stack,  fetches a 32-byte word from the block-scoped transient storage at that `slot` for the executing contract, and pushes the value on top of the stack. If no value has been written to that slot in the current block, the value returned is 0.
```

author: jochem-brouwer

Hiya, some editorial comments!

From a review point of view: this introduces a new feature which adds context making transactions non-parallelizable (the block storage can change between transactions) which is a problem since https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-7928 introduces parallelizable transactions in the protocol. Adding BLOAD/BSTORE to the Block Access List (BAL) would put strain on networking. However, since storage writes/loads are part of the BAL, such block-level scoped warm/cold storage might actually be possible 🤔
