pr_title: Update EIP-7756: Move to Draft
author: Copilot
body: `registerEndpoint` is `payable` and also takes `(token, grossAmount)`, but the spec doesn’t define the ETH-vs-ERC20 payment rules (e.g., whether `token == address(0)` implies `msg.value == grossAmount`, or how ERC-20 transfers are performed). Please normatively specify the payment path, required invariants on `msg.value`, and how `grossAmount` is measured (requested vs actually received, fee-on-transfer tokens, rounding for the 1% fee).

pr_title: Update EIP-7756: Move to Draft
author: Copilot
body: The fee rule “collect `grossAmount × 1 %`” needs a precise rounding definition (floor/ceil, minimum fee, and handling small `grossAmount` values) to avoid divergent implementations. Please specify the exact integer math (e.g., `fee = grossAmount * QUIC_FEE_BPS / 10_000`) and expected rounding behavior.

pr_title: Update EIP-7756: Move to Draft
author: Copilot
body:
`deregisterEndpoint` requires a reentrancy guard, but the spec should also require checks-effects-interactions ordering (delete/zero the stored bond and endpoint state before transferring ETH/ERC-20) to prevent reentrancy even in implementations that use different guard patterns. Also clarify how the bond is returned for ERC-20 vs ETH.
```suggestion
MUST release the locked 99 % bond back to `msg.sender`. For ETH-denominated bonds this MUST be implemented as an ETH transfer to `msg.sender` performed after all state changes; for ERC-20-denominated bonds this MUST be implemented as an ERC-20 token transfer from the contract to `msg.sender` performed after all state changes.  
MUST delete the endpoint record and zero out any stored bond or related accounting associated with `msg.sender` **before** performing any external calls or transfers (i.e., follow the checks-effects-interactions pattern).  
MUST emit `EndpointDeregistered(agent)`.  
MUST use a reentrancy guard around this function in addition to the checks-effects-interactions ordering described above.
```

pr_title: Update EIP-7756: Move to Draft
author: Copilot
body: This change repurposes EIP-7756 from an existing proposal (previously about EOF/EVM tracing) into an unrelated QUIC transport registry. In the EIPs process, an assigned number generally shouldn’t be overwritten for a different standard; this should be submitted as a new draft file (e.g., `eip-draft_*.md`) and let editors assign a new number, or otherwise coordinate an official takeover with the prior EIP’s authors/editors.

pr_title: Update EIP-7756: Move to Draft
author: Copilot
body: The header `requires: 165` doesn’t include ERC-20 even though the specification explicitly allows bonding with ERC-20 tokens. Please reference ERC-20 (EIP-20) in the document and add it to `requires` so dependencies are explicit and consistent with the template.

pr_title: Update EIP-7756: Move to Draft
author: Copilot
body:
Hardcoding a single `OPACUS_TREASURY` address in a standards-track ERC makes the spec chain/deployment-specific and forces all implementations to route fees to one recipient. Consider specifying the fee recipient as a constructor parameter / governance-controlled variable, or defining a mechanism to update it, so independent deployments can still be ERC-7756-compliant.
```suggestion
| `OPACUS_TREASURY` | `implementation-defined` | Protocol/governance-controlled fee recipient address |
```

pr_title: Update EIP-7756: Move to Draft
author: Copilot
body: The ERC-165 requirement uses a hardcoded interface id `0x51554943` ("QUIC"), but ERC-165 interface IDs are defined as the XOR of function selectors for a specific interface. Please define an explicit `IERC7756` interface and specify the correct ERC-165 interface id (or how to derive it), otherwise different implementations will not interoperate on `supportsInterface`.

pr_title: Update EIP-7756: Move to Draft
author: Copilot
body: The reference implementation link points to `../contracts/ERC7756QuicTransport.sol`, but this repository doesn’t contain a `contracts/` directory, so the link is currently broken. Please either add the referenced implementation under the repo (commonly under `assets/eip-7756/` for larger code) or include a minimal reference implementation inline, per the EIP template guidance.

pr_title: Update EIP-7756: Move to Draft
author: Copilot
body:
The document is missing the required `## Copyright` section and CC0 notice that EIPs in this repository include (see `eip-template.md`). Please add the standard copyright/CC0 text at the end so the spec meets repository submission requirements.
```suggestion
See [`contracts/ERC7756QuicTransport.sol`](../contracts/ERC7756QuicTransport.sol).

## Copyright

Copyright and related rights for this EIP are waived via [CC0](https://creativecommons.org/publicdomain/zero/1.0/).
```

pr_title: Update EIP-7756: Move to Draft
author: Copilot
body:
`discussions-to` should point to a specific discussion thread for this ERC (e.g., an Ethereum Magicians topic URL), not a user profile page, so reviewers can track design discussion and consensus.
```suggestion
discussions-to: https://ethereum-magicians.org/t/erc-7756-quic-transport-registry-standard/12345
```

pr_title: Update EIP-7756: Move to Draft
author: Copilot
body:
The abstract says the 1% registration fee is collected "via" the `X-Opacus-QUIC` header convention, but the fee is an on-chain side effect of `registerEndpoint` while the header is an off-chain signalling mechanism. Please reword to avoid implying the HTTP header is part of (or required for) the on-chain fee collection.
```suggestion
ERC-7756 specifies an on-chain registry for QUIC/HTTP3 agent transport endpoints. Agents register by staking a bond in ETH or ERC-20 tokens; **1 % of the bond is collected as a protocol fee** by the registry contract at registration time. A standardised `X-Opacus-QUIC` signalling header convention allows HTTP/3 peers to advertise and discover endpoints that are registered on-chain. Consumers discover peers by latency budget, transport mode, or kernel-bypass capability, enabling sub-millisecond, physically-routed multi-agent communication over HTTP/3 and eBPF/XDP paths.
```

pr_title: Update EIP-7756: Move to Draft
author: Copilot
body: The RFC 2119 keyword boilerplate is incomplete vs the repository’s EIP template (it omits keywords like REQUIRED/SHALL/etc and RFC 8174, and doesn’t link the RFCs). Please align this paragraph with the standard wording from `eip-template.md` to avoid ambiguity in normative language.

pr_title: Update EIP-7756: Move to Draft
author: Copilot
body: `TransportMode` includes `KernelBypass`, but `Endpoint` also has a separate `bool kernelBypass`. This allows inconsistent states (e.g., `mode == Standard` while `kernelBypass == true`) and duplicates semantics used by discovery methods. Consider representing kernel-bypass capability in exactly one place (either as a mode value or as an independent capability flag) and defining how it maps to the HTTP header.

pr_title: Update EIP-7756: Move to Draft
author: Copilot
body:
`registeredAt` / `updatedAt` are specified as `uint64` but the spec doesn’t define what they represent (e.g., `block.timestamp` seconds, block number, or something else). Please specify the exact source and unit so implementations and indexers are consistent.
```suggestion
    uint64        registeredAt;      // UNIX timestamp in seconds (`block.timestamp`) when this endpoint was first registered
    uint64        updatedAt;         // UNIX timestamp in seconds (`block.timestamp`) when this endpoint was last updated (equals `registeredAt` on creation)
```

pr_title: Add EIP: Withdrawal credentials preregistration
author: jochem-brouwer
body:
```suggestion
This EIP introduces a preregistration mechanism that allows a validator key holder to commit to specific withdrawal credentials before any deposit is made, addressing a known deposit front-running vulnerability in delegated staking. Preregistrations are submitted through a new [EIP-7685](./eip-7685.md) request type via a system contract on the execution layer, rate-limited by an [EIP-1559](./eip-1559.md)-style exponential fee mechanism. The consensus layer stores the preregistration in beacon state and enforces it at deposit processing time: matching deposits proceed and the preregistration is consumed; mismatched deposits are silently rejected. The mechanism is fully optional — deposits for public keys without a preregistration are processed exactly as today.
```

author: avsetsin
body: Good catch! The original text was confusing. What I meant: 4 per block is the dequeue cap (max requests popped from queue into the block), not the submission cap. There is no per-block limit on submissions, only gas limits them. But every submission in a block increases count, and at block end excess += count − target. So a burst of many submissions in one block spikes the fee starting from the next block. The "3 per block" scenario only applies if exactly 4 requests are submitted per block. Updated the text to make this clearer.

pr_title: Update EIP-8070: Update EIP-8070
author: healthykim
body:
Just a nitpick, but I think the categories could be structured as follows:

1. Building on full blobs
: This strategy only includes blob transactions for which the client has the full blob data when building an execution payload. To support higher blob throughput, the CL client may update its notified custody to Union(data indices, its own custody column indices), 2-3 slot ahead of being proposer.

2. Building on partial blobs
: This requires further risk profiling, so we can defer including it for now.

So in strategy 1, the EL client always builds the payload based on the existing includable transactions for which it has full blob data. Whether the number of those txs should be maximized by eagerly fetching cells is up to the CL client's decision. I personally think this is clearer from the implementation perspective

pr_title: Update EIP-8070: Update EIP-8070
author: healthykim
body:
I have two questions regarding this part

1. Is this different from the process currently required to submit a private blob transaction?
I think this paragraph is intended to show that we can better support private blob transactions, since we can seed columns without providing full blobs, enabling pre-propagation of blob data, something that wasn’t possible before this proposal. If that was the intention, I don’t think it is emphasized enough.

2. Can we actually provide this property?
First, if the builder is the only one announcing full availability, the blob cannot be sampled, since it does not pass the availability check.
Second, the proposal seems to say two contradictory things, “For maximal security, you can choose to drop transactions that do not appear to be available among peers / resample them / apply peer scoring to drop peers that frequently refuse fetch requests,” and “Private blobs can be pre-propagated without revealing their full content.” Even if the builder successfully pre-seeded its peers, those columns would not likely to be propagated beyond them, and will be dropped because those peers cannot see enough availability around them. If a peer requests a full fetch with prob. p, the builder would refuse to respond, which may lead to disconnection depending on the client’s design.

Aside from this, I think providing multiple options is a good thing. However, the options specified in the EIP should be things that are mutually consistent and have concrete use cases. If there are too many “may”s, it becomes difficult for both us and client teams to reason about all the possible combinations. So I’d like to take a closer look at the heuristics described below and related things to see whether some of them can be omitted, so that we can reason about those combinations more concisely.

pr_title: Update EIP-8070: Update EIP-8070
author: kamilsa
body:
> Building on full blobs
I clarified that builders should act as providers at least 2-3 slots ahead of the block they are building (or simply act as provider permanently)

> Building on partial blobs

I don't see how builders can include partial blobs into their bids. Builders should possess all the columns, as once they see their block bid is approved they need to propagate them to the column subnets

pr_title: Update EIP-8070: Update EIP-8070
author: healthykim
body:
> Before assembling an execution payload, a local block builder MUST switch its fetch policy to eager mode

What I meant to say is that we can relax this requirement, not making it strictly mandatory. Builders could construct a block based on the p portion of blob transactions that are fully available in their blobpool, and they could also maximize candidate transactions by switching to eager mode. The former option could be attractive for solo stakers with limited network resources.

> I don't see how builders can include partial blobs into their bids. Builders should possess all the columns, as once they see their block bid is approved they need to propagate them to the column subnets

Builders could rely on the assumption that the partial blobs they are including are already widely propagated at the EL level, and that other nodes could retrieve and propagate those blob data via the getBlobs engine API (after the execution payload is revealed). However, we currently don't have a theoretical analysis to determine to what extent and under which conditions these assumptions hold.

pr_title: Update EIP-8070: Update EIP-8070
author: healthykim
body:
I don’t see why this should be included here. How is it relevant to the sparse blobpool? Also, this is something well-known and clients are already mitigating. Not including non-includable blob transactions is already an obvious principle in current transaction pool design in general.

The suggested attack is also not specific to sparse blobpool and already possible under the current pool, and it can be done not only through fees but also via various ways like low nonce.

I don’t think this needs to be mentioned in this EIP as a separate heuristic. If it is necessary, it could be included as one of the possible approaches for peer scoring part. And I this this has already been mentioned there.

pr_title: Update EIP-8070: Update EIP-8070

author: kamilsa

pr_title: Update EIP-8070: Update EIP-8070
author: raulk
body:
Dynamically switching to eager mode reveals that we're about to become a builder. We should avoid this as it weakens builder privacy and can become an attack vector.

Also, the CL has no way of informing the EL about its builder status / schedule, so we'd need to add something to the Engine API if we wanted to go this way.

Instead, I suggest that local builders run in "eager mode" _permanently_, but capped to `USER_CONFIGURED_MAX_BLOBS_PER_BLOCK` introduced in EIP-7872.

The blobpool would hold full `USER_CONFIGURED_MAX_BLOBS_PER_BLOCK` pending blobs at all times.

Depending on the value of that flag and the current blobpool traffic, p=0.15 might already satisfy the requirement. If not, we'd top up above p=0.15 to the amount necessary to meet the threshold at all times.

pr_title: Update EIP-8070: Update EIP-8070
author: healthykim
body:
```suggestion
The sparse blobpool mechanism brings sampling to the EL as well, with an anticipated ~4x reduction in average bandwidth consumption for a given blobpool load. In doing so, it preserves the unstructured, stochastic nature of the current blobpool rather than introducing complex sharding architectures, prioritizing simplicity and resilience. Moreover, it preserves the CL's ability to satisfy its own sampling needs with the pre-propagated data in the EL blobpool (through the `getBlobs` Engine API). This is achieved by aligning the EL and CL sampling, in particular by having the EL fetch the cells corresponding to the CL custody set. This preserves a key feature of the blobpool, as it stretches the time window for blob data propagation, offloading this work from the critical path of block validation and leading to smoother and less bursty bandwidth utilization patterns over time.
```

pr_title: Add EIP: Scheme-Agile Transactions
author: SamWilsn
body:
```suggestion
This scheme achieves quantum safety by making each secp256k1 key pair single-use. At account creation, the user derives a deterministic sequence of key pairs (e.g. via [BIP 44]) and commits to all future public keys by constructing a Merkle tree over their hashes. The Merkle root is embedded in the sender address. Each transaction provides a standard ECDSA signature plus a Merkle proof that the signing key is the leaf at position `nonce` in the committed tree.

[BIP 44]: https://github.com/bitcoin/bips/blob/69a63f629f4c27b249882b4e0db6af516f1bcea9/bip-0044.mediawiki
```

pr_title: Add EIP: Scheme-Agile Transactions
author: SamWilsn
body:
```suggestion
| Secret | Location | On-chain exposure |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [BIP 39] seed | User's device only | Never |
| `sk_i` (ephemeral private key) | Derived on-the-fly for nonce `i` | Never (public key exposed for exactly one transaction) |
| `merkle_root` | Encoded in the address, carried in witness | Fully public by design |
| `merkle_tree` | User's device (or recomputable from seed) | Per-transaction proof is public |

[BIP 39]: https://github.com/bitcoin/bips/blob/69a63f629f4c27b249882b4e0db6af516f1bcea9/bip-0039.mediawiki
```

pr_title: Add EIP: EVMification
author: jochem-brouwer
body:
(review note, not editor note): This is a very important point, as this removes the standard-warm status in [EIP-2929](https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-2929) for precompiles. This thus also makes the first call per transaction `COLD_ACCOUNT_ACCESS_COST` (2600 as of Osaka) higher, which I think is something to consider. I would assume that if the EVM code is audited, that most/all clients will redirect calls to a faster implementation rather than running the EVM bytecode, thus implicitly having the precompile in a fast cache.
But this is an improvement made over time, so for simplicity indeed move this to non-precompiles first.

pr_title: Add EIP: EVMification
author: jochem-brouwer
body:
(review note, not editor note): Note that if this happens after [BALs](https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-7928) are introduced this adds an extra item to the BAL of the fork block.
Note that this also raises the maximum theoretical size of the BAL by one (due to the code entry which is not paid for by gas), so this https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-7928#block-access-list-size-constraint might not hold for the fork block in theory (would need some analysis later)

pr_title: Update EIP-8141: add mempool policy
author: nerolation
body:
The EIP-8141 mempool rules may be overly strict, e.g. (from the EIP):

`SLOAD` can be used only to access `tx.sender` storage, including when reached transitively via `CALL*` or `DELEGATECALL`.

**Privacy tools may need paymasters that verify SNARKs and check nullifier/root state from external pool contracts, all within the VERIFY frame. This wouldn't work as-is.**

I've been thinking about it more and came up with 3 possible solutions to "solve" this:

1st option, having a standardized privacy paymaster: Nodes recognize it by code match and exempt it from storage access restrictions. Paymaster can read from any pool. Pools stay flexible, paymaster is fixed.

2nd option, using state witnesses: User brings merkle proofs for the storage they need (root membership, nullifier non-membership). Validation checks proofs against a recent state root. It might also need to restrict for which contracts you can "bring" your state + mpt proofs (which makes it worse than option 1 if no better solution here) and another downside is that it comes with more calldata, thus bigger and more expensive.

3rd option, having a standardized pool interface: Pools implement a standard interface (`isValidRoot`, `isNullifierSpent`). Nodes can whitelist pool addresses (otherwise there could be malicious pools implementing the correct interface to drain the paymaster). Any paymaster can call these and pools are constrained + paymasters stay flexible. In case a pool behaves maliciously, nodes automatically block it (no social intervention needed). This is similar to option 1 but keeps the paymaster more flexible.

All of them may also need the 100k gas limit to be raised to make SNARK validation withing VERIFY possible, which might be fine if we restrict it to standardized contracts or interfaces.
My feeling is that option 1, while taking some flexibility from paymasters, might be the best.

Why TSTORE/TLOAD banned if transient storage is cleared between frames? 
Shall we ban semi-deprecated opcode CALLCODE?
Should CALLs with value > 0 be banned? Or maybe this is already caught by `execution performs a state write`?

I am thinking of non-standard setups where we would use tricks to still mass-invalidate transactions, for instance doing a CALL with value to create an account, and then using this change of state to: CALL a helper contract with a specific amount of gas, if this succeeds/fails then diverge on the execution logic. We can now use the just-created account for this. If CALLs with value is banned then we can use the CREATE2 on the deterministic deployer contract and use the just-created contract as a way to mass-invalidate.

Of course this can be mitigated by only allowing very specific transactions in the mempool (also think that this is the general idea here?).

The deterministic deployers - is this a *general* deterministic deployer, or rather a specific deterministic deployer which only creates very specific contracts in a deterministic matter? Otherwise this state write could be abused? (EXTCODESIZE)

pr_title: Add EIP: Cryptographically Agile Transactions
author: xinbenlv
body:
This example section currently makes the chaining rule a little hard to follow for me. I may be misreading it, but the inconsistency seems to be between the normative formula in the Specification section and the illustrative bullets here in the rationale.

The formal rule at L124 says:
- payload_commitment = CA_TX_TYPE || rlp(payload_type) || rlp(payload_body)
- signature_hash(0) = keccak256(payload_commitment)
- signature_hash(i) = keccak256(payload_commitment || prior sig pairs...)

So for the first few signatures, I would expect something like:
- index 0: keccak256(payload_commitment)
- index 1: keccak256(payload_commitment || rlp(sig_type_0) || rlp(sig_body_0))
- index 2: keccak256(payload_commitment || rlp(sig_type_0) || rlp(sig_body_0) || rlp(sig_type_1) || rlp(sig_body_1))

But the examples in this rationale section do not seem to match that cleanly:
- The index-1 bullet appears to say hash(payload_commitment || payload_commitment || ...), which reads as though payload_commitment is included twice.
- The index-2 bullet appears to say hash(CA_TX_TYPE || payload_commitment payload_commitment || ...), which may be malformed in two ways:
- it seems to switch from payload_commitment back to CA_TX_TYPE || ..., even though payload_commitment already includes CA_TX_TYPE
- it also seems to repeat payload_commitment again, and may be missing a separator between terms

I may be misunderstanding the intended shorthand here, but if not, I think these illustrative bullets may contain copy/editing issues rather than reflecting a different rule. If so, could they be rewritten to exactly mirror the normative formula above? That would make it much easier for readers to confirm they understand what each signer is hashing.

> Hi! I think we want to reserve the ability to define custom behavior in 8141 default contract and we don't want to rely on another EIP / precompile like this.

Could you please clarify your concern? Is it that EIP-8141 should remain fully self-contained or about the dependency risk of EIP-7932?

EIP-8141 already depends on EIP-7951 for P256 verification, depending on EIP-7932 is no different in principle. EIP-8030 (part of 7932) also fixes the [malleability issue](https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-7951#malleability:~:text=of%20RIP%2D7212.-,Malleability,requiring%20non%2Dmalleability%20should%20implement%20additional%20checks%20at%20the%20application%20layer.,-Side%2DChannel%20Resistance) with EIP-7951.

If you are concerned with the dependency chain that would be created, a soft dependency on EIP-7932 with a specific `signature_type` byte for EIP-7932 signatures would still allow for accounts to use EIP-7932 **only** if it is *also* included within a fork, preventing EIP-7932 blocking EIP-8141.

pr_title: Update EIP-8141: Simplify approval bits so that accounts don't have to manipulate them
author: 0xrcinus
body:
I'm a bit confused by these bits. They feel redundant and only narrowly useful.

If the frame target is not the `sender`, only payment approval is valid (only the sender can approve execution)
If the mode is `SENDER`, only payment approval is valid (execution approval is already in place, or the `SENDER` frame would have reverted already)

If the mode is `VERIFY` and the frame.target is `sender`, then indeed execution and payment could be approved - and the original PR https://github.com/ethereum/EIPs/pull/11401 suggests that this is the motivation:

> allowing the user to specify to their own account what should be approved

But why put this in the mode as these extra bits, rather than just putting it into the `data` for the frame? (indeed the EOA default code suggests that the approval scope should be in the first nibble of the first byte).

pr_title: Update EIP-8141: Simplify approval bits so that accounts don't have to manipulate them
author: derekchiang
body:
@0xrcinus the EOA default code is out of sync with the rest of the spec.  Indeed the primary motivation for moving the intended approval scope off `frame.data` is to simplify the account -- we realized that if the scope was part of `frame.data`, since `frame.data` is elided from the sighash calculation, the account would have to calculate a "real sig hash" with `keccak(sighash | scope)` and then check the signature against that.  So it's a lot of repetitive logic that every account would have to implement.

Therefore by moving scope into the non-elided part of the transaction, we can simplify the account so that it's "just a signature check against sighash".  The exact mechanism for communicating the intended scope is still being researched though; this PR is just one of the proposals.

pr_title: Update EIP-8141: Simplify approval bits so that accounts don't have to manipulate them
author: 0xrcinus
body:
> @0xrcinus the EOA default code is out of sync with the rest of the spec.  Indeed the primary motivation for moving the intended approval scope off `frame.data` is to simplify the account -- we realized that if the scope was part of `frame.data`, since `frame.data` is elided from the sighash calculation, the account would have to calculate a "real sig hash" with `keccak(sighash | scope)` and then check the signature against that.  So it's a lot of repetitive logic that every account would have to implement.
> 
> Therefore by moving scope into the non-elided part of the transaction, we can simplify the account so that it's "just a signature check against sighash".  The exact mechanism for communicating the intended scope is still being researched though; this PR is just one of the proposals.

Thanks that makes sense. On reflection I think this can still go towards simplicity rather than adding more fields that need to be populated correctly, which feels fragile. 

For example, what if... 

- APPROVE could only be called in VERIFY frames (I think this is reasonable as since VERIFY frames are a staticcall, it's essentially equivalent to appending to any other kind of frame)
- maximum of two VERIFY frames per txn
- if there is just one VERIFY frame in a txn, it needs to approve execution and payment (if it calls APPROVE)
- if there are two, the first has to approve execution (i can't think of a good reason why you would want to approve payment first), then the second can only approve payment

In that way you can infer simply by the number of VERIFY frames which can approve which scope. 

If there is an argument for more than two VERIFY frames (maybe some kind of fallback payment logic, seems spurious to me) - you could still support that by assuming all VERIFY frames after the first can only approve payment

Maybe worth discussing in a wider forum, would be keen to understand where to join the conversation

pr_title: Update EIP-8141: Simplify approval bits so that accounts don't have to manipulate them
author: derekchiang
body:
@0xrcinus If I'm understanding your suggestion correctly, you are saying that `APPROVE` doesn't even need to take a `scope` operand, because the scope can always be determined from the frame structure alone, right?

But that seems like it would make reasoning about smart contract code quite difficult.  If I'm auditing a contract and it just calls `APPROVE` without an explicit scope -- how do I know what the contract is trying to do?  Is it approving payment or gas?  That sounds like a security issue.

Or perhaps you are saying that, the smart contract would introspect its own position in the frame list, and based off that it'd call `APPROVE` with the correct scope?  Feels like that'd make the contract code quite ugly unless 1) the protocol enforces certain frame structures (e.g. two maximum VERIFY frames and they all have to be at the top), 2) we make the introspection mechanism more powerful, so that the contract can ask questions like "is there a gas-paying VERIFY frame under me?"  I'm not sure if 1 would make the protocol too rigid, and also not sure how to cleanly do 2.

In general though, I definitely agree that the approval bits mechanism doesn't feel super elegant and there may be a better solution.  

Re public discussion, [the Ethereum Magician thread](https://ethereum-magicians.org/t/eip-8141-frame-transaction/27617) is pretty active.  There's also a semi-public TG group but I couldn't find an invite link, but if you tell me your TG I can invite you to it.  Also the coauthors do read these PR comments.  I for one really appreciate your feedback so far!

author: forshtat

> consecutive `SENDER_ATOMIC` frames revert together

Controlling execution flow based on frame flags and position in a transaction might be confusing while not giving all the flexibility we may need for EOA batches.

Is there a real need for this seemingly EOA-centric feature in the EIP?

pr_title: Update EIP-8141: add support for atomic batching
author: 0xrcinus
body:
> Is there a real need for this seemingly EOA-centric feature in the EIP?

Multiple SENDER frames introduce native batching at the protocol level, so I think there is an argument that it should be the preferred way to batch calls for all accounts (which is to say, I think that this is relevant for smart accounts too - why would you have custom batching capabilities in a smart account rather than just using multiple frames? This allows smart accounts to focus on authorization and authentication)

pr_title: Update EIP-8141: add support for atomic batching
author: pedrouid
body:
Maybe I'm missing something here but wouldn't we want SENDER to always be atomic by default

Most use-cases that I can imagine benefitting from Frame transactions would always be atomic

Even the non-atomic use-cases will likely be better suited as multiple Frame transactions instead

Basically my point is that instead of adding a SENDER_ATOMIC... we should just make SENDER atomic

pr_title: Update EIP-8141: add support for atomic batching
author: derekchiang
body:
@pedrouid there are real use cases where you don't want frames to be atomic.  The main thing to recognize is that frames can inspect the status of one another.  For example, you can have a SENDER frame that executes on the condition that another frame succeeded (or failed).  A more concrete example would be a SENDER frame that claims some tokens from a DeFi protocol, and then another SENDER frame executes to swap the tokens into ETH if and only if that frame succeeded.  So in these cases, you want the frames to be non-atomic.

I also think there's the more general point that non-atomicity is more "general" than atomicity -- non-atomicity is basically the OR behavior and atomicity is the AND behavior, and in all programming languages AND always takes a higher precedence than OR.  So having top-level frames being OR by default while providing support for AND on top of that seems to be more elegant to me than the other way around.

pr_title: Update EIP-8141: add support for atomic batching
author: frangio
body: The main use case I've heard for non-atomic frames is using ERC-20 for gas payment. The payer needs the guarantee that once it has accepted payment, the next frame will do an ERC-20 transfer and not revert.

pr_title: Update EIP-8141: add support for atomic batching
author: forshtat
body:
> Maybe I'm missing something here but wouldn't we want SENDER to always be atomic by default

Strong arguments were made both for and against atomic by default.

But, what I am saying is that I would suggest a "do or do not, there is no try" approach to configurable atomicity.
For example, with positional flags this PR proposed, if you had two atomic groups in a batch you would need to insert a no-op call frame just to break the `SENDER_ATOMIC` sequence, would you not?

pr_title: Update EIP-8141: add support for atomic batching
author: derekchiang
body:
I have completely reworked the atomic batching mechanism based off the "mode flags" mechanism introduced by @fjl [yesterday](https://github.com/ethereum/EIPs/pull/11401).  Credit of the idea goes to @sm-stack, but basically we use a bit flag to indicate that the current frame is atomic with the next frame.  So for example, if you want to have two consecutive batches like @forshtat said, then you would do:

- SENDER (flag set)
- SENDER (not set)
- SENDER (flag set)
- SENDER (flag set)
- SENDER (not set)

In this case, frame 1-2 are one batch, and frame 3-5 are another batch.  That way the batch boundaries are cleanly separated.

Also this PR is based off [another PR](https://github.com/ethereum/EIPs/pull/11404) for handling approval bits so it contains some changes not related to batching, so the plan is to merge the other PR first.

pr_title: Add EIP: snap/2 - BAL-Based State Healing
author: nerolation
body:
Snap v2 should be fully independent of `eth/71`, only requiring the EIP-7928 block header.

* `eth/69` and `eth/70` peers transmit headers as raw RLP: they would carry the new header field after the fork.
* `snap/2` defines its own `GetBlockAccessLists` / `BlockAccessLists` messages (`0x06` / `0x07`), explicitly duplicating the BAL exchange from `eth/71`. The rationale (EIP-8189, line 92) states that this is to “avoid coupling sync functionality to eth”.

Therefore, `snap/2` obtains everything it needs from:

* **EIP-7928:** the header field for validation and the BAL format definition
* **Its own messages:** BAL fetching

However, there's then a flaw in the current wording. Line 106 states:
“snap/2 peers must also run `eth/71` or later, as snap is a dependent satellite of eth.”

This requirement should be removed to avoid confusion.

pr_title: Add EIP: snap/2 - BAL-Based State Healing
author: mirgee
body:
Could we assign new message codes to the newly added messages rather than reusing codes of the removed messages?
* `GetBlockAccessLists` -> `0x08`
* `BlockAccessLists` -> `0x09`

Besu implementation currently assumes that `message code`, as opposed to the pair `(message code, protocol version)`, uniquely identifies the message type, which has been true in the recent `eth` protocol versions.

There is already a precedent for increment-only approach in the `eth` protocol: In `eth/67`, `GetNodeData` (`0x0d`) and `NodeData` (`0x0e`) were removed . Then, in `eth/69`, `BlockRangeUpdate` was added and instead of reusing the space created by the removal, it used a new message code (`0x11`). There are also precedents for reusing message codes, but arguably those are older.

Some of the benefits of the increment-only approach:
* potentially simpler implementation because of no clashing of message types over message codes
* message codes order message types by the order they were introduced
* related message types may use nearby message codes

What are the drawbacks?

author: weiihann
body:
Yes that's a good point. We can always update this parameter whenever slot time changes, so there's an added dependency which could be annoying.

Using timestamp would also work. But clients internally manage state on a per-block basis, rather than using timestamp. Further investigations are needed, so for now, I'd prefer to keep it this way.

pr_title: Add EIP: State Tiering by Write Age
author: weiihann
body: Yes it's a deliberate choice. Read-only keys will not enjoy the benefit of prefetching (unless clients have some internal mechanism to do so). There are still some optimization paths, such as preloading the active parts of the database and trie node paths to active leaves.

pr_title: Add EIP: Foundations of EVM Control Flow
author: gcolvin
body: Proposals to provide for static control flow have repeatedly been rejected at very late stages in our process.  EIP-2315 was actually removed from the code of a fork that was ready to ship.  One reason for these years of wasted effort is that too many people in the community simply don't understand the very wide range of relevant industry experience and computer science.  Computer architecture, graph theory, interpreters, compilers, formal analysis, blockchain security, cryptography, zero knowledge and more are all relevant, and people cannot be expected to be experts in all of them.  I'm not.  I do not want to see the current proposals fail for the same reasons.  Therefore I insist on explaining the issues in a prominent, permanent document that can be carefully reviewed by experts and linked to by the proposals themselves.

pr_title: Add EIP: Foundations of EVM Control Flow
author: gcolvin
body:
The very long and consistent historical context is an important part of my argument.  I'm not justifying a new idea.  I'm discussing the application of some of the oldest ideas in computer science to Ethereum.  So I need to present a very brief history of the relevant computer architecture and science, and I'm starting from the beginning -- it's that simple.

The sentences at issue here were in fact already merged as part of the Motivation for EIP-7979.  I moved them here so that EIP-7979 would be more technically focused.  I'm not sure why that refactoring has created controversy where there previously was none.

pr_title: Update EIP-8037: clarify reservoir mechanics
author: misilva73
body:
@rakita had a [comment](https://github.com/ethereum/EIPs/pull/11292#discussion_r2816007050) on this that I think we should think through.

When a `CALL` (or `DELEGATECALL`/`CALLCODE`) is made, the caller specifies a single gas value `g`. With multidim metereing, we need to figure out three things:

1. **Forwarding**: How much of `gas_left` and `reservoir` does the subcall receive?
2. **Success**: How are unused portions returned?
3. **Failure**: What happens on REVERT vs. exceptional halt (OOG)?

Here is a map of some options and their pros and cons.

## Option 1: Forward all reservoir; return reservoir on any failure (this is the proposal from @rakita )

**Mechanics:**

- Subcall receives: `call_gas_left = min(g, 63/64 * caller.gas_left)`, `call_reservoir = caller.reservoir` (all of it)
- On **success**: return unused `call_gas_left` and unused `call_reservoir` to caller
- On **REVERT**: return unused `call_gas_left` and unused `call_reservoir` to caller
- On **exceptional halt**: consume `call_gas_left` (zeroed), return unused `call_reservoir` to caller

**Rationale for returning reservoir on halt:** State changes are reverted on failure, so no state was actually grown — the state gas wasn't "consumed" in any economic sense.

**Pros:**

- Subcalls have full access to state gas — large contract deployments via factories work without issues
- Reservoir is never "wasted" on failures, which is consistent with the principle that state gas pays for *long-term* state growth (which didn't happen)
- Simple forwarding logic (just pass it all through)
- Enables the full benefit of uncapped state gas in nested calls

**Cons:**

- The gas limit `g` no longer bounds total spending — a subcall to an untrusted contract can consume unbounded state gas from the caller's reservoir
- Breaks composability expectations: callers cannot limit how much state gas a subcall uses
- Existing patterns that use gas limits for economic protection (e.g., limiting gas sent to an external callback) become insufficient
- A malicious or buggy callee can drain the caller's entire reservoir even though the caller only intended to send `g` gas

## Option 2: Forward all reservoir; consume reservoir on exceptional halt (this is the current proposal)

**Mechanics:**

- Subcall receives: `call_gas_left = min(g, 63/64 * caller.gas_left)`, `call_reservoir = caller.reservoir`
- On **success**: return unused `call_gas_left` and unused `call_reservoir`
- On **REVERT**: return unused `call_gas_left` and unused `call_reservoir`
- On **exceptional halt**: consume **both** `call_gas_left` and `call_reservoir` (zeroed)

**Pros:**

- Consistent with current EVM behavior where exceptional halts consume all forwarded gas
- Provides a strong penalty for OOG, discouraging underestimation of gas
- Full reservoir access for subcalls

**Cons:**

- Extremely punishing — a single OOG in any subcall wipes the entire transaction's remaining state budget
- Makes calling untrusted contracts very risky (they can force-burn your reservoir by triggering OOG)
- Same composability problem as Option 1 (caller can't bound subcall state gas usage)
- The punishment is arguably disproportionate since no state was actually grown

## Option 3: Forward reservoir proportional to gas fraction; return reservoir on failure

**Mechanics:**

- Subcall receives: `call_gas_left = min(g, 63/64 * caller.gas_left)`, `call_reservoir = caller.reservoir * (call_gas_left / caller.gas_left)`
- On **success**: return unused portions of both
- On **REVERT**: return unused portions of both
- On **exceptional halt**: consume `call_gas_left`, return unused `call_reservoir`

**Pros:**

- The gas parameter `g` provides *proportional* control over both dimensions — sending half your gas sends half your reservoir
- Better composability: callers retain reservoir proportional to gas they didn't forward
- More predictable total spending (bounded by ~2× the gas fraction sent)
- Callers can limit exposure to untrusted contracts

**Cons:**

- State-heavy subcalls may be starved of reservoir (e.g., a factory deploying a 24kB contract needs a high gas limit even if regular gas usage is low)
- The proportional split may not match actual needs — some calls are 90% state, others 0%
- Adds calculation complexity and potential rounding issues
- Nested calls compound the problem: at depth N, the available reservoir may be heavily fragmented

## Option 4: Forward reservoir capped at `g`; return reservoir on failure

**Mechanics:**

- Subcall receives: `call_gas_left = min(g, 63/64 * caller.gas_left)`, `call_reservoir = min(g, caller.reservoir)`
- On **success**: return unused portions of both
- On **REVERT**: return unused portions of both
- On **exceptional halt**: consume `call_gas_left`, return unused `call_reservoir`

**Pros:**

- The gas parameter `g` sets a clear bound: total spending in the subcall ≤ 2g (at most `g` from each pool)
- Symmetric and intuitive — "I'm sending `g` worth of resources in each dimension"
- Callers retain excess reservoir beyond `g`
- Reasonable composability: gas limit still gives meaningful spending control
- Subcalls get enough reservoir for most use cases (the gas limit is usually set high enough to cover the call's needs)

**Cons:**

- A subcall can still spend up to 2× the gas parameter `g` (potentially surprising)
- For very state-heavy operations, the cap may be too restrictive — e.g., deploying a large contract from a factory may need reservoir >> regular gas
- Somewhat arbitrary choice to cap at exactly `g` (why not 2g? or g/2?)
- Doesn't solve the problem of deploying contracts larger than `TX_MAX_GAS_LIMIT` worth of state gas from within a subcall

## Summary

| | Reservoir forwarded | Spending bound | Factory/nested state ops | Composability |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Option 1**: Forward all, return on fail | All | Unbounded | Full support | Poor |
| **Option 2**: Forward all, consume on halt | All | Unbounded | Full support | Very poor |
| **Option 3**: Proportional forward | Proportional | ~2× fraction | Partial | Good |
| **Option 4**: Capped at `g` | min(g, reservoir) | ≤ 2g | Partial | Good |

The fundamental tension is between **reservoir accessibility in subcalls** (needed for factory patterns and nested contract deployments) and **caller control over spending** (needed for composability with untrusted code). Options 1-2 maximize accessibility but sacrifice control while Options 3-4 attempt a middle ground. Either way, I think option 2 is too punishing and agree with @rakita that option 1 > option 2. The question is whether we want to add more control to caller gas spending by having option 3 or 4.

A future option to consider is introduce an explicit two-parameter call through a new opcode.

**Mechanics:**

- Introduce new CALL variants (e.g., `CALL2D`) or extend EOF call instructions to take two gas parameters: `regular_gas` and `state_gas`
- Subcall receives: `call_gas_left = regular_gas`, `call_reservoir = state_gas`
- Legacy CALL opcodes use a default policy (e.g., Option 3 or 4) for backward compatibility
- On **success/REVERT/halt**: handle each dimension independently per the chosen policy

**Pros:**

- Most explicit and flexible — callers have full control over both dimensions
- No ambiguity about behavior; no surprising interactions
- Can be introduced alongside EOF without breaking legacy contracts
- Future-proof: works cleanly if more dimensions are added later (per EIP-8011)

**Cons:**

- Requires new opcodes or changes to the EVM instruction set
- Legacy contracts cannot benefit — only new contracts using the new opcodes
- Increases EVM complexity (more opcodes, more edge cases)
- EOF adoption timeline is uncertain; legacy contracts may dominate for years
- Two gas parameters add UX complexity for developers and tooling

pr_title: Update EIP-7928: simplify capping of block-level access list
author: nerolation
body:
With EIP-7981, the true minimum cost per BAL item is `COLD_SLOAD_COST = 2100`. Using 2000 in the formula gives slack of:

```                                                                                                              
slack = gas_limit // 2000 - gas_limit // 2100                                                                              
     ≈ gas_limit × (1/2000 - 1/2100)
     = gas_limit × 100 / (2000 × 2100)
     = gas_limit / 42,000
```

Another option would have been to use the 2100 in the formula but then we'd have to somehow account for the 87 items that could go into the BAL for free (which requires constants that we only have on the CL + is less future proof than the 100 gas buffer):

| System Call                      | Addresses | Storage Keys                          | Items |
|----------------------------------|-----------|----------------------------------------|-------|
| EIP-4788 beacon roots            | 1         | 2 writes                               | 3     |
| EIP-2935 history storage         | 1         | 1 write                                | 2     |
| EIP-7002 dequeue (16 reqs)       | 1         | 4 headers + 3×16 queue reads           | 53    |
| EIP-7251 dequeue (2 reqs)        | 1         | 4 headers + 4×2 queue reads            | 13    |
| EIP-4895 withdrawals             | 16      |              -               | 16    |
| **Total**                        | **20**     | **67**                                 | **87**|

author: jochem-brouwer
body:
```suggestion
bal_items <= block_gas_limit // ITEM_COST
```

pr_title: Update EIP-7928: simplify capping of block-level access list
author: jochem-brouwer
body: I think it should be ~~motivated~~ clarified here that `ITEM_COST` is the lowest gas cost which could be paid to add an entry to the BAL. (It is in this case thus the tx access list cost + gas warm access and not cold_sload of 2100)

pr_title: Update EIP-7928: simplify capping of block-level access list
author: jochem-brouwer
body:
```suggestion
`ITEM_COST` reflects the sum of `ACCESS_LIST_STORAGE_KEY_COST` (1900, as defined in [EIP-2930](./eip-2930.md)) and `WARM_STORAGE_READ_COST` (100, as defined in [EIP-2929](./eip-2929.md)). The `storage_keys` is the total number of storage keys across all accounts, and `addresses` is the total number of unique addresses accessed in the block.
```

pr_title: Update EIP-7928: simplify capping of block-level access list
author: nerolation
body:
valid point, let me think out loud here:

Accessing an address costs 2400 gas + 100 gas at minimum. 
Accessing a storage slot costs 1900 gas + 100 gas as minimum.

An attacker crafts an invalid block with a BAL containing as many items as possible that still passes the item count constraint. The transactions in the block would then do heavy execution (otherwise, if they would actually access those items, it's fine and it's just a valid block).

The hypothesis is that using 2000 gas even for addresses (as done right now) might be overly forgiving to invalid blocks that could be invalidated earlier.

### With the current formula:
With a 150M gas limit, the attacker would put `150M//2_000=75_000` addresses into the BAL.
The initial check wouldn't fail but clients would be able to invalidate the block after executing the first (max-size) transaction in the block (thanks to [the other invalid BAL check](https://github.com/ethereum/EIPs/pull/11223) we have introduced).

### With your proposed formula:
With a 150M gas limit, the attacker would put `150M//2_500=60_000` addresses into the BAL.
Same as before, it would take the execution of one (max-size) transaction to invalidate the block.

So essentially, the non-consensus check introduced in PR #11223 would prevent the DoS early on. Thus, the attack is effectively prevented.

The per-tx gas-budget check (PR #11223) is the actual defense against bloated BALs, and it catches invalidity after a single transaction regardless of whether the item count used 2000 or 2500. For consistency with #11223 it would make sense to just use 2000.

pr_title: Update EIP-8024: Switch to branchless normalization and extend EXCHANGE
author: frangio
body:
If we use the same domain as `decode_single`, we either have a discontinuity in the pairs that can be represented[^1], or there would be two ways to encode the same pair. So the range is reduced to keep this a bijection. We could try to map the extra available domain to some other continuous section but I figured the complexity wasn't worth it.

[^1]: You'd be able to swap 11,16 and 11,18 but not 11,17.

pr_title: Update EIP-8024: Switch to branchless normalization and extend EXCHANGE
author: r0qs
body:
Thanks a lot @frangio :)

I have a question about the EXCHANGE depth check. If I understand correctly, the forbidden range implicitly ensures that `decode_pair` always produces `n < m` (with max `n = 14`, max `m = 29`). This invariant can be inferred from the `encode_pair` precondition, but not as a postcondition of `decode_pair`. Since the depth check only validates `m`, I believe it would be valuable for implementers to know that `decode_pair` also guarantees `n < m`, otherwise `stack[top - n]` could be an out-of-bounds access.

Would it make sense to either change the depth check to be defensive
```suggestion
    5. If `max(n, m) + 1 > len(stack)`, halt with exceptional failure.
```

Or, since `decode_pair` should always produce `n < m`, maybe add an assert to make the invariant explicit like in `encode_pair`?

```python
  def decode_pair(x: int) -> tuple[int, int]:
      # ...
      if q < r:
          n, m = q + 1, r + 1
      else:
          n, m = r + 1, 29 - q
      assert 1 <= n < m <= 29 and n + m <= 30
      return n, m
```

pr_title: Update EIP-8024: Switch to branchless normalization and extend EXCHANGE
author: r0qs
body: Oh sorry, my mistake. I thought the diff showed you removing the assertion on the input `x` rather than modifying it. So asserting the result seems unnecessary.

pr_title: Update EIP-8024: Switch to branchless normalization and extend EXCHANGE
author: frangio
body:
I still think there is an opportunity to make this clearer, though I prefer to keep the instruction spec as it is now. See https://github.com/ethereum/EIPs/pull/11351

By the way I realized with the new EXCHANGE it's much simpler to check whether a pair is swappable. Basically just `n + m <= 30`.

pr_title: Add EIP-8005 draft
author: poojaranjan
body:
@BitmineMarine , 
As much as the intent behind proposing a new standard in the Ethereum repository is appreciated, it’s important to have a process in place for all contributors. Just as editors have responsibilities, authors do as well. These processes are designed to make collaboration smoother and proposals easier to review over time.

**To support new or less technical contributors**, in addition to [EIP-1: EIP Purpose and Guidelines](https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-1), we’ve recently added a [CONTRIBUTING.md](https://github.com/ethereum/EIPs/blob/master/CONTRIBUTING.md) guide, which we believe will help document and prepare a proposal.

Before submitting a PR, it is strongly advised to first share the idea on the [Ethereum Magicians](https://ethereum-magicians.org/) Forum, or on the [Ethereum Research](https://ethresear.ch/) Forum if the idea relates to new or research-oriented technical changes. Early discussion helps refine the proposal and gather community feedback before editorial review.

In addition, we host [EIP Editing Office Hours](https://github.com/ethereum/pm/issues/1912) every Tuesday at 16:00 UTC. You’re very welcome to join and ask questions directly to the editor on call. If the timing isn’t convenient, you can also add your questions to the agenda and follow the recording afterward.

I’d encourage you to incorporate the suggestions above while preparing the PR for editor review. If bandwidth or technical formatting is a constraint, you’re also welcome to collaborate with a “champion” who can help document and move the idea forward.

Appreciate your consideration for enhancing the Ethereum ecosystem.

from the networking perspective it's faster to erasure encode and then reconstruct, but independently (since this requires networking optimizations) the abs data load of sending the payload vs. the payload blob is the same and nothing changes with respect propagation time. It's not cell level sampling - at first, one would probably have validators download the full payload (but from blobs), in a next step one could move to sampling - like like with 4844 -> peerdas. 

Today, proposing blocks and getting them out in time is critical and it feels wrong to 2x upload data and propagating the same data twice. The blobs should fully replace the ExecutionPayload in the beacon block, or, after 7732, deprecate the ExecutionPayloadEnvelope.

author: frisitano
body:
> from the networking perspective it's faster to erasure encode and then reconstruct,

Why is this? Isn't there a computational overhead in the reconstruction stage? 

> It's not cell level sampling - at first, one would probably have validators download the full payload (but from blobs), in a next step one could move to sampling - like like with 4844 -> peerdas.

Where are the blobs stored, and where do the validators download them from? If I'm not mistaken, in PeerDAS, clients currently only have custody of columns (I may be mistaken here). Would it be gossiped over the EL blob pool? 

> Today, proposing blocks and getting them out in time is critical and it feels wrong to 2x upload data and propagating the same data twice. The blobs should fully replace the ExecutionPayload in the beacon block, or, after 7732, deprecate the ExecutionPayloadEnvelope.

I agree we should minimise redundancy. However, only re-execution nodes (or nodes interested in the full execution payload) would subscribe to the execution payload topic. zk attesters would only sample columns (or, in the future, cells).

pr_title: Update EIP-8142: rebase on top of 7732
author: nerolation
body:
> Why is this? Isn't there a computational overhead in the reconstruction stage?
This is because you can better parallelize propagation. Today we are naive sending the full data to 8 (or more) peers when proposing a block This means as the proposer, your load is quite significant because of the multiplier.
It's faster to erasure encode the data, and send smaller packets around. Reconstructing is faster than having the remaining 49% propagate. 

> Where are the blobs stored...
This is up to clients. EL clients that keep all could just reconstruct the EL block from the payload blobs.
Other nodes that don't keep all (which might happen 1-2 forks after the initial rollout - just my feeling), would probably handle the columns as they handle type-3 tx columns today.


Imo, it's wrong to think of zkEVM as this one time event that happens within one fork. I'm more thinking of it as a transition over multiple forks. First do optional proofs, then BiB, then mandatory proofs and then BIB with sampling.
In this picture we would have redundancy of the payload data between BiB and mandatory proofs, which means, if we enforce proposers to broadcast their blocks over blobs + in the executionpayloadenvelope, then we have to scale the gas limit down as the total upload for the proposer doubles.

pr_title: Update EIP-8142: rebase on top of 7732
author: nerolation
body:
Yeah that's my thinking too.
BiB is big and won't happen at the same time with mandatory proofs.
If I had to chose, I'd do optional proofs -> BiB without sampling -> mandatory proofs (everyone still downloads all payload blobs) -> BiB sampling.

before introducing mandatory proofs it's worth to have proofs (optional) + BIB in place already and see how it's doing before shipping mandatory proofs.

pr_title: Update EIP-8142: rebase on top of 7732
author: frisitano
body:
I agree with an iterative approach across forks and with minimising bandwidth overhead.

What I’m trying to understand is the concrete protocol: specifically, how payload blob gossip would work end-to-end. Without a precise specification, it’s hard to evaluate whether the bandwidth savings hold in practice.

For example, if a node that needs the full payload must download ~50% of all columns to reconstruct it, the effective bandwidth savings may diminish. In that case, reconstruction becomes relatively expensive and may skew toward higher-resource nodes.

Could you clarify what the exact protocol flow is that achieves lower bandwidth and latency via the blobs-only route?

pr_title: Update EIP-8142: rebase on top of 7732
author: nerolation
body:
There are no bandwidth savings in that sense as erasure encoding would e.g. 2x the size but you only need 50% for reconstruction. The promise is that it's faster.
This question doesn't impact BiB too much though. We can just assume that payloads through blobs are as fast (not slower but also not faster at first) as payloads in envelopes. 

The flow would be like:
Builder constructs block + proof -> block_to_blob -> propagate -> attesters download all blobs.
The only thing that changes compared to today is that blocks are first encoded into blobs.

author: frisitano
body:
> There are no bandwidth savings in that sense as erasure encoding would e.g. 2x the size but you only need 50% for reconstruction. The promise is that it's faster. This question doesn't impact BiB too much though. We can just assume that payloads through blobs are as fast (not slower but also not faster at first) as payloads in envelopes.

My understanding is that the current blob gossip mechanism on the CL operates via columns. If that’s the only available path, then reconstructing payload blobs would require fetching ~50% of all columns, which contain additional type-3 blob data. Under that model, reconstructing the payload blobs may, in practice, effectively require downloading all blobs (including type-3 blobs). Am I reasoning about that correctly, or is there a more efficient retrieval path being assumed here?
 
> The flow would be like: Builder constructs block + proof -> block_to_blob -> propagate -> attesters download all blobs. The only thing that changes compared to today is that blocks are first encoded into blobs.

When you say “propagate,” could you clarify the exact path or topic?

pr_title: Update EIP-8142: rebase on top of 7732
author: nerolation
body:
I don't think we would go to column sampling right at the beginning. Just like 4844 a first step would be putting blocks into blobs but no column sampling yet.
I think you're conflating type-3 blobs with payload blobs which are just two different object that just happen to share the same encoding. No need to commingle those ever: a column in payload blobs would be a column in a different matrix than 4844 blobs (at least initially bc it's an interesting thought to put them together but adds tons of complexity and not even sure it ever makes sense.)

One could propagate all payload blobs through the same payload_blob_sidecar topic.

pr_title: Update EIP-8142: rebase on top of 7732
author: kevaundray
body:
> at least initially bc it's an interesting thought to put them together but adds tons of complexity and not even sure it ever makes sense

Why and where does it add complexity?

pr_title: Update EIP-8142: rebase on top of 7732
author: nerolation
body:
I was thinking because those are very different. One of them is a user-facing DA guarantee whereas the other is a protocol DA guarantee. Not storing (and therefore not being able to provide samples) for type-3 tx blobs is different than not storing execution payloads.
E.g. a full node will store all payload blobs but doesn't need to store all type-3-tx blobs.

pr_title: Update EIP-8142: rebase on top of 7732
author: frisitano
body:
From my understanding, the primary objective of BiB is to provide a DA guarantee for payload data that allows zk attester nodes to verify availability without downloading the full payload.

If we simply place payloads into blob sidecars without introducing sampling, it’s not immediately clear to me how that advances this objective. In that scenario, we would be adding an additional layer of indirection and protocol complexity without yet enabling lightweight DA verification for zk attesters.

My current view is that a pragmatic approach would be to:
- Add payload blobs to the existing matrix and leverage the established sampling mechanism, and
- In parallel, guarantee full payload availability via the PTC on the opt-in execution_payload topic.

This would allow us to achieve the DA objective in the near term, while keeping the door open to later separating payload blobs into an independent sampling scheme if that proves beneficial. Alternatively, if cell-level sampling lands quickly, we may not need to split them at all.

I do recognise that this introduces additional redundancy and bandwidth overhead for builders. If the bandwidth overhead isn't prohibitive, then one could argue the redundancy is actually a good thing, whilst BiB is still experimental.

pr_title: Update EIP-8142: rebase on top of 7732
author: nerolation
body:
> If we simply place payloads into blob sidecars without introducing sampling, it’s not immediately clear to me how that advances this objective. In that scenario, we would be adding an additional layer of indirection and protocol complexity without yet enabling lightweight DA verification for zk attesters.

It doesn't advance the objective initially but it's a first BIG step. The DA guarantee would initially be the same but instead of everyone downloading the ExecutionPayloadEnvelope, everyone would download all blobs.

> isn't prohibitive
Imo this redundancy is a clear non-starter. Bandwidth is already the biggest constrain today. ePBS will make the time available for building even tighter. BALs won't help builder. Then, optional proofs are super big too.

If BiB is shipped it shouldn't be experimental anymore but fully replace the existing path. At the beginning it might even be shipped without any zk cryptography and only with mandatory proof the zk proof required for block-to-blob encoding could be introcuded.

pr_title: Update EIP-8142: rebase on top of 7732
author: frisitano
body: Makes sense. I think it would be helpful to define the high-level design for each milestone that gets us to our objective.

pr_title: Update EIP-8142: rebase on top of 7732
author: nerolation
body:
yeah agree!

If I had to steelman a timeline it i'd say:

1) optional proofs -> get a sense for proofs, their size, proof generation, proof delivery, etc.
2) Bib -> put transactions into the payload, comes with "big" changes on the CL, EL keeps operating as-is, explore payloads as blobs instead of one monolithic payload, no erasure encoding, no column-wise sampling, everyone downloads all payload blobs, fully deprecate ExecutionPayload, no block-to-blob encoding proof needed since everyone downloads everything.
3)  mandatory proofs -> move ALL attesters to use proofs instead of re-execution. payload size will go up with the gas limit increases
4) BiB with sampling

(4) could be done at the same time as (3) or even before - no strong opinion here. But it feels wise to do BiB without changing anything on the EL at first. CL downloads all payload blobs, constructs and ExecutionPayload from it and uses the existing engine  api methods to send it to the EL.

pr_title: Add EIP: Private Key Deactivation Aware ecRecover
author: colinlyguo
body:
Thanks for the feedback. I'd prefer to keep the "return 32 zero bytes" behavior rather than switching to an execution failure. Here's the reasoning:

`ecRecover` already uses `address(0)` as its failure sentinel. Invalid signatures, malformed `v`, out-of-range `r`/`s`, all of these return 32 zero bytes with `success = 1`. Deactivation is semantically another form of "recovery failed," so mapping it to the same sentinel is reasonable.

Changing to `success = 0` would break existing callers. Many deployed contracts wrap `ecRecover` with low-level `staticcall` and `require(success)`, assuming the precompile never execution-fails. Introducing a new execution-failure path would turn "signature didn't verify" into "entire transaction reverts" for those callers.

pr_title: Update EIP-7723: Move to Living
author: abcoathup
body:
> Living makes sense as a process doc

My preference is final.  If we want to change the inclusion stages again we should have a new EIP.

pr_title: Update EIP-7723: Move to Living
author: nixorokish
body: "Living" aligns better with its mostly closely related EIP, EIP-1. Why freeze the inclusion stages when they can be descriptive of a process that is evolving to find the most efficient path? Freezing them adds unnecessary bureaucracy and makes people feel like they have to conform reality to rules that described a process at a snapshot, but may not be the most efficient process now. Requiring that a whole new EIP gets written seems really unnecessary

pr_title: Update EIP-7723: Move to Living
author: abcoathup
body:
> Why freeze the inclusion stages when they can be descriptive of a process that is evolving to find the most efficient path?

The EIP only covers the inclusion stages and guidance on the stage transitions.  It doesn't dictate the process beyond this. e.g. It doesn't cover headliners at all.  Which gives plenty of scope for the process to evolve without changing the inclusion stages.

**The EIP process should work for the core devs (and not the other way around).  So I won't oppose making this living.**

I generally dislike living EIPs as they need to be maintained and we don't know who the future maintainers will be in years to come.  e.g. the OG author is moving on from L1 R&D.

I'm concerned about capture, which in my view, appears easier with modifying a living EIP compared with have to convince core devs to adopt a completely new EIP.

pr_title: Update EIP-7723: Move to Living
author: poojaranjan
body:
With due respect, before debating the “EIP status”, I would argue that the EIP itself is confusing in its current form.

The Motivation states: _“This EIP proposes definitions for the various stages EIPs go through when planning network upgrades.”_

However, throughout the document, the term “status” is used interchangeably with “stage”, which creates ambiguity.

To be clear:
- EIP status refers to the standardization and review lifecycle of an EIP.
- EIP stages refer to the network upgrade planning and deployment process.

These are two distinct concepts, and conflating them risks long-term confusion, especially for new contributors and readers of the specification.

This may have been missed earlier, but it can still be corrected. There is an [open PR](https://github.com/ethereum/EIPs/pull/11006) addressing this inconsistency. I would request the authors to review it and **either merge it if appropriate, or explicitly explain the rationale for rejecting it**.

The purpose of progressing through EIP statuses is to enable review and convergence. A clear response from the authors, whether to accept or close earlier PR before responding to this change, would help keep the process moving forward.

pr_title: Update EIP-7723: Move to Living
author: poojaranjan
body:
> "Living" aligns better with its mostly closely related EIP, EIP-1. Why freeze the inclusion stages when they can be descriptive of a process that is evolving to find the most efficient path? Freezing them adds unnecessary bureaucracy and makes people feel like they have to conform reality to rules that described a process at a snapshot, but may not be the most efficient process now. Requiring that a whole new EIP gets written seems really unnecessary

I understand the concern about adding extra process, and I agree that rules should not force people to follow an outdated snapshot of reality.

That said, **EIP** stands for _Ethereum **Improvement** Proposal_. If something is meant to be treated as a standard process, it needs to be clearly defined and moved to `Final` status. When the situation changes, **writing a new EIP is completely reasonable**. It helps clearly document what changed and why, which is useful for future contributors.

Editors have always preferred **lightweight EIPs,** and I support creating new EIPs when needed instead of stretching existing ones beyond their original scope.

**Regarding EIP-7723 blocking the Fusaka Meta EIP**: similar to what was done for Pectra Meta EIP, it does not need to be listed as required considering the process is still experimental. In that case, **EIP-7606 can still move to `Final` status** and status for EIP-7723 can be discussed separately.

author: chatgpt-codex-connector[bot]
body:
**<sub><sub>![P2 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P2-yellow?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Fix executor test that contradicts TBA.execute access**

Test 2 asserts that an executor can call `execute(...)` directly on the TBA, but earlier the spec explicitly states standard ERC‑6551 TBAs only allow the NFT owner to call `execute()` and that executors must call the identity contract directly. In a self‑owning setup the owner is the TBA itself, so the test case would fail for a compliant ERC‑6551 implementation and conflicts with the guidance above. This inconsistency can mislead implementers about the required TBA behavior or make the test suite impossible to satisfy without a custom TBA.

Useful? React with 👍 / 👎.

pr_title: Add EIP: Self-Sovereign Agent NFTs
author: chatgpt-codex-connector[bot]
body:
**<sub><sub>![P2 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P2-yellow?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Avoid bricking executors by configuring after self-transfer**

The setup sequence transfers the NFT to its own TBA before configuring an executor. If `setExecutor` is gated by NFT ownership (the common and safest choice), then after step 3 there is no externally controlled signer who can call `setExecutor`, so the agent cannot ever grant its first executor and the token is effectively locked. The spec should either require configuring executors before the self‑transfer or define an explicit bootstrap mechanism that can still authorize the first executor once the NFT is self‑owned.

Useful? React with 👍 / 👎.

> Thoughts on also adding an absolute limit using the following static pre check:

> ```python
> assert len(bal.storage_reads) <  (BLOCK_GAS_LIMIT - TX_COUNT * TX_BASE_COST ) // 2000

yes, something like this should be done independently as a consensus rule. I'd have it more general and focus on all unique entries of the BAL instead of only storage keys:

assert (

    + len({address for (address, _, _, _, _, _) in bal})
) * 2000 <= BLOCK_GAS_LIMIT - TX_COUNT * TX_BASE_COST

pr_title: Update EIP-7928: Clarify anti-dos measure for invalid, bloated BALs
author: marioevz
body:
I think having this as part of "Security Considerations" instead of directly within spec is a slippery slope.

The `SHOULD` wording here makes this very hard to test because we are now leaving something that invalidates a block up to the implementer, which could make some clients reject a block while others accept it.

Also the `remaining block gas` mentioned below is not very well defined IMO.

Is it:
- Block gas limit minus the gas consumed by all transactions prior to the one currently being processed.
or
- Total block gas used minus the gas consumed by all transactions prior to the one currently being processed.

If it's the second one, it could pose a problem for blocks with zero transactions because `G_remaining` is zero, because the block uses no gas, while the `R_remaining` is non-zero due to the storage accesses in the system contract transactions.

> I don't have a strong opinion here, let me know what you think

To take a step back and state the objective of BiB as I see it: BiB aims to leverage execution proofs to minimise the network bandwidth required by zk attesters when gossiping execution payloads.

The principle is that any payload data that is not required to advance the consensus-layer state may be cryptographically committed to, made available via blobs, and verified indirectly via execution proofs.

Under the current protocol, transaction data appears to be the only component of the execution payload that is not required for consensus-layer progression. Following the BAL fork, it may be possible to apply the same treatment to BALs, but I'm not super familiar with the CL spec for BALs.

pr_title: Add EIP: Block-in-Blobs (BiB)
author: nerolation
body:
Regarding "how" to put the transactions into the blob, I think it'd be be useful to encode the transactions into the following indexed blob format:

```
Header (12 bytes)
  [0:2]   num_tx (uint16)
  [2:4]   num_wd (uint16)
  [4:8]   tx_data_size (uint32)
  [8:12]  wd_data_size (uint32)

Tx Index (4 * num_tx bytes)
  [12 + 4*i]  offset of tx[i] in tx data section

Wd Index (4 * num_wd bytes)
  offset of wd[i] in wd data section

Tx Data
  concatenated raw transactions

Wd Data
  concatenated withdrawals (44 bytes each)
```

This structure is enough to find the exact blob/cell(s) in which a certain transaction is encoded.
  
I checked ~600 recent blocks and this adds ~1% overhead on avg (in relation to worst-case blocks it be less than 0.1%) that comes from the mapping in the first cell. Also, transactions usually fit in one cell:

| Cells | Count | Percent |
|-------|-------|---------|
| **1** | **485** | **82.1%** |
| **2** | **87** | **14.7%** |
| 3 | 10 | 1.7% |
| 4+ | 9 | 1.5% |

**96.8% of transactions fit in 1-2 cells**

pr_title: Add EIP: Block-in-Blobs (BiB)
author: frisitano
body:
Gloas introduces an `execution_payload` topic [here](https://github.com/ethereum/consensus-specs/blob/master/specs/gloas/p2p-interface.md#execution_payload).

In practice, I don't think that it would be very common for a payload to be reconstructed from blobs. If a node wanted the payload, then it would be more efficient to subscribe to the `execution_payload` topic.  

There is one edge case that comes to mind in the case of a malicious builder. In the context of mandatory proofs with a super majority of stake operating zk validators, which only listen to header topics (e.g. `execution_payload_header`), it would be possible for the builder to only publish the payload in blobs and then gossip the execution payload header (they do not gossip the full execution payload on the `execution_payload` topic). The execution payload header and payload bobs would be sufficient for zk validators, and as such, a super majority would attest. Any validators (or builders) depending on the full execution payload from the `execution_payload` topic would not be able to progress. As such, to mitigate this issue, the nodes would need to fall back to reconstructing from blobs. Alternatively, we could introduce "bridge nodes" which always reconstruct the full execution payloads from blobs and then gossip on the `execution_payload` topic to proactively mitigate this grief attack.

- When we snarkify this, the validator would only have the ExecutionPayload header, so having `payload_blob_count` would allow them to know how many blobs the payload occupies

- The blobs are constructed in newPayload using the ExecutionPayload, this function then eventually calls validate_block and that takes an EL block as input. For the second point, we could compute the payload blobs in `validate_block` which would allow us to compute the correct `blob_gas_used` without having a parameter in the header, but since engine_newPayload needs to check the version hashes before calling validate_block, I think we would need to propagate those back up by adding the commitments/version hashes into the header.

pr_title: Add EIP: Block-in-Blobs (BiB)
author: frisitano
body:
To clarify, I’m not proposing that payload blobs be directly referenced by transactions, nor that transactions adopt literal type-3 semantics. I’m suggesting that transactions should continue to pay for data availability as they do currently with the calldata fee, but that the calldata fee be reinterpreted as a DA fee priced against blob gas.

In BiB, where transaction data is made available via blobs, the existing calldata fee no longer accurately reflects the underlying DA resource being consumed. My proposal is therefore to charge each transaction a DA fee proportional to its data size, using a blob gas derived per-byte price.
